title: The Life of a Request on the Server
objectives: Trace a request through proxy, middleware, handler and data store
Place timeouts and limits at each hop
Find where time goes in a slow request

cards.title: From socket to response
cards.body: A request passes through layers before your code sees it: a load balancer or reverse proxy, the server’s connection handling, a chain of middleware (logging, authentication, parsing), the route handler, and the calls it makes to databases or other services. The response travels back through the same layers.

cards.title: Worked example: where 480 ms went
cards.body: Timing each stage turns “the API is slow” into a specific fix.
steps: Assume: a request to load an order page, timed per stage
Proxy and TLS: 5 ms; authentication middleware: 15 ms
Handler runs 12 database queries one after another at 35 ms each: 420 ms
Serialising the response: 40 ms
cards.note: Result. 480 ms in total, of which 420 ms is twelve sequential queries. Fetching the same data in one or two queries matters far more than tuning the other stages.

cards.title: One request, layer by layer
cards.body: Each layer can reject a request early, which is cheaper than failing deep inside.
steps: Reverse proxy: terminate TLS, enforce body size limits, forward
Middleware: request id, logging, authentication, parsing
Handler: validate input, run the business logic
Data calls: queries and requests to other services, each with a timeout
Response: status, headers and body back out through the middleware

cards.title: Timeouts at every hop
cards.body: Every outbound call needs a timeout, and inner timeouts should be shorter than outer ones. If the proxy gives up after 30 s but the handler waits 60 s on a database, the server keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for.

cards.title: Trap: no request id
cards.body: Without an id generated at the edge and passed to every log line and downstream call, the logs for one slow request are scattered among thousands of others. Add the id first, before any other middleware runs.

cards.title: Edge case: the client hangs up mid-request
cards.body: If the client disconnects or its proxy times out, most servers keep running the handler to the end: database queries, payment calls and all. Proxies often log this separately (nginx records status 499, “client closed request”). Pass cancellation or a deadline down through every call so abandoned requests stop consuming database time.

questions.prompt: Which concern belongs in middleware rather than in each handler?

choices.label: Choosing which rows a report returns
Formatting a single product’s description
Checking the session on every authenticated route
Calculating the price of one order

questions.explanation: Cross-cutting concerns that apply to many routes belong in middleware.

questions.prompt: The proxy times out after 30 s; the handler’s database call has no timeout. What happens on a hung query?

choices.label: The client gets a timeout while the server keeps holding resources for the query
The database timeout defaults to the proxy’s 30 seconds
The request succeeds later, once the hang finally ends
The proxy cancels the database query for you automatically

questions.explanation: Outer timeouts do not cancel inner work; set inner timeouts shorter than outer ones.

questions.prompt: A handler makes 12 sequential queries at 35 ms each. What is the best first fix?

choices.label: Increase the proxy timeout
Compress the response
Add more middleware logging
Fetch the data in one or two queries

questions.explanation: Twelve round trips dominate; cutting them saves most of the 420 ms.

questions.prompt: Where should an oversized 2 GB upload to a JSON endpoint be rejected?

choices.label: At the proxy or first parsing layer, by a body size limit
In the database when the row is too large
In the handler after the whole body is parsed
In the client’s browser only

questions.explanation: Rejecting early avoids reading and buffering the whole body.

questions.prompt: Order the layers an incoming request passes through.

items.label: Authentication middleware
Route handler
Request id and logging middleware
Database query
Load balancer or reverse proxy

questions.explanation: Edge first, cross-cutting middleware next, business logic and data last.

questions.prompt: A handler calls three services in sequence (40 ms, 60 ms, 100 ms). If the three calls are independent and made in parallel instead, about how many milliseconds does that part take?
assumptions: Calls are independent
Parallel time is set by the slowest call
questions.explanation: Design implication: parallel calls cut this step in half, but the slowest dependency now sets the latency, so its timeout and tail latency matter most.

flashcards.front: Why generate a request id at the edge?
flashcards.back: To tie every log line and downstream call for one request together.
Inner timeouts shorter than outer ones.
About as long as the slowest one.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

mechanism.title: What happens between accept and response
steps: The connection: a client connects to a load balancer or reverse proxy, which often terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP (or re-encrypted HTTP) to an application server. The proxy also enforces limits such as maximum header and body size and idle timeouts.

The server: a listening process accepts the connection and hands each request to a worker: a thread, a process, or an event loop callback, depending on its concurrency model. If all workers are busy, requests wait in a queue, and that wait counts towards the user’s latency.

Middleware: a chain of functions wraps every request. Typical order: assign a request id, start a timer and log, enforce rate limits, authenticate, parse the body, then call the handler. Each piece can end the request early with an error.

The handler: it validates input, applies business rules and calls data stores and other services. Every call it makes is a network round trip with its own latency and failure modes, so the number of calls and whether they run in sequence or parallel decide most of the time spent.

The response: the handler returns a status, headers and body; middleware adds headers, logs the outcome and records metrics such as duration and status class. The proxy may compress the response and keep the client connection open for the next request.
Deadlines: a request has a total time budget. Passing the remaining budget to downstream calls (rather than giving each a fixed long timeout) stops work continuing after the caller has given up.

useWhen: Put cross-cutting concerns (ids, logging, auth, limits) in middleware so every route gets them.
Measure each stage of a slow request before changing anything.
avoidWhen: Avoid outbound calls without timeouts; a hung dependency ties up workers indefinitely.
Avoid doing expensive work before cheap checks; reject bad requests at the edge.

numbers.title: A latency budget for one endpoint
assumptions: Target: 95% of requests under 300 ms (an example objective)
Fixed costs: proxy and middleware about 20 ms
Two independent downstream calls, each about 80 ms at the 95th percentile
steps: Sequential calls: 20 + 80 + 80 = 180 ms, leaving 120 ms for the database and rendering.
Parallel calls: 20 + 80 = 100 ms, leaving 200 ms.
Give each downstream call a timeout below the remaining budget, for example 150 ms, so one stuck call cannot use the whole 300 ms.
Adding a third sequential call of 80 ms would eat two-thirds of the remaining slack in the sequential design.
numbers.result: Writing the budget down shows which calls must run in parallel and what timeout each can afford.

india.title: Cascading failures in the Google SRE book
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s chapter on cascading failures describes how requests that keep running after their callers have timed out waste capacity and spread overload. It recommends propagating deadlines: each request carries an absolute deadline, and each layer checks the remaining time before starting work or calling a dependency. That is the deadline idea in this lesson, applied across many services.

pitfalls.trap: “The API is slow, so we need a bigger server.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d time each stage first; it is often many sequential queries or one slow dependency.”

pitfalls.trap: “The load balancer timeout protects us.”
pitfalls.say: “It stops the client waiting, but the server keeps working; inner calls need shorter timeouts or deadlines.”

takeaways: Requests pass through proxy, middleware, handler and data calls, and back.
Put ids, logging and auth in middleware.
Every outbound call needs a timeout shorter than its caller’s.
Sequential round trips usually dominate latency.

interactive.title: Where do the 480 ms go?
interactive.prompt: An order page takes 480 ms. Proxy and TLS take 5 ms, auth middleware 15 ms, response serialisation 40 ms, and the handler makes 12 database queries one after another at 35 ms each. Which change helps most?

choices.label: Load the data in one or two queries
choices.feedback: Right: twelve sequential queries take 420 ms of the 480.

choices.label: Speed up serialisation
choices.feedback: At most 40 ms to gain.

choices.label: Remove the auth middleware
choices.feedback: Saves 15 ms and removes a security check.

interactive.reveal: Measure, then attack the biggest stage. Here sequential round trips to the database dominate; batching them (or a join) cuts most of the latency.

Reverse proxies at the edge

title: Sessions and Stateless Servers
objectives: Explain what “stateless server” means in practice
Compare server-side sessions with self-contained tokens
Handle logout and revocation in each design

cards.title: State lives somewhere
cards.body: HTTP itself does not remember previous requests. A login therefore has to be carried on every request, either as a session id that points at data stored on the server side, or as a signed token that contains the data itself.

cards.title: Misconception: stateless means no state at all
cards.body: A stateless server keeps no per-user state in its own memory between requests. The state still exists, in a shared session store, a database or a signed token, so any server can handle any request.

cards.title: A server-side session from login to logout
cards.body: The browser holds only a random id; the data stays on the server side.
steps: Login succeeds: create a random session id and store {user, expiry} under it
Set the id in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie
Each request: look up the id in the shared session store
Logout: delete the entry; the id is useless from then on

cards.title: Self-contained tokens
cards.body: A signed token carries claims such as the user id and expiry. Servers verify the signature without a lookup, which saves a round trip, but a token stays valid until it expires unless you keep a revocation list, which brings back a lookup.

cards.title: Trap: sessions in server memory
cards.body: Keeping sessions in one server’s memory works until there are two servers or a restart. Then users are logged out or bounce between servers that do not know them. Use a shared store, or sticky routing only as a temporary measure.

cards.title: Edge case: session fixation
cards.body: If the session id stays the same before and after login, an attacker who planted a known id in the victim’s browser (for example through a crafted link on a site that accepts ids from the URL) is logged in as the victim once they sign in. Issue a fresh session id at login and at every privilege change, and accept ids only from cookies.

questions.prompt: What makes a web server “stateless” in this sense?

choices.label: It keeps no per-user data in its own memory between requests
It forgets the user after every single page
It never reads anything from a database
It does not use cookies at all for anything

questions.explanation: State moves to a shared store or the request itself, so any server can answer.

questions.prompt: A user clicks “log out everywhere”. Which design makes this simplest?

choices.label: Tokens stored in the browser only
Sticky sessions on one server
Server-side sessions: delete the user’s session entries
Long-lived signed tokens with no revocation list

questions.explanation: Deleting server-side entries invalidates them immediately.

questions.prompt: What should a session cookie contain in a server-side session design?

choices.label: The user’s id and role in plain text
The full shopping cart
A long random id with no meaning on its own
The user’s password hash

questions.explanation: The id is a pointer; the data stays on the server side.

questions.prompt: Why are short expiry times common for self-contained access tokens?

choices.label: Signatures become invalid after a few minutes anyway
Shorter-lived tokens are smaller to send each time
They cannot be revoked without a lookup, so a short life limits the damage
Browsers delete stored tokens after 15 minutes

questions.explanation: Short lives plus refresh tokens balance revocation against lookups.

questions.prompt: Order a server-side session’s life.

items.label: Delete the entry on logout
Verify the password
Create a random session id and store the session data
Send the id in a hardened cookie
Look up the id on each request

questions.explanation: The id is created at login and destroyed at logout.

questions.prompt: Login sessions for a web app with 6 servers behind a load balancer.
constraints: Admins must be able to force logout
Any server may receive any request
One extra lookup per request is acceptable

approaches.label: Long-lived signed tokens only
Server-side sessions in a shared store
Sessions in each server’s memory

rationaleOptions.label: Every server reads the same store, so routing does not matter
Signed tokens can be revoked by deleting them from the server
Deleting the entry logs the user out immediately

rationaleConflicts.r3: The server does not hold them; revocation needs a separate deny list.

questions.explanation: When revocation matters and a lookup is affordable, server-side sessions are the simple choice.

flashcards.back: No per-user data in its own memory between requests; state lives in a shared store or the request.
Session: random id, data in a store, easy revocation. Token: data inside, no lookup, hard to revoke.

flashcards.front: Why not keep sessions in memory?
flashcards.back: Restarts and multiple servers lose or split them.

mechanism.title: How login state follows a user across requests
steps: After a successful login, the server needs a way to recognise the same user on the next request. HTTP gives two carriers: cookies, which the browser sends automatically, and headers such as Authorization, which the client sets itself.

Server-side sessions: the server generates a long, unpredictable session id (OWASP suggests at least 64 bits of entropy), stores session data under it in a shared store such as a database or an in-memory key-value store, and sends only the id to the client. Every request costs one lookup.

Self-contained tokens: the server signs a set of claims (user id, roles, expiry) and sends the whole token. Any server with the verification key can check it without a lookup. The data is visible to anyone holding the token unless it is also encrypted, so it should not contain secrets.

Revocation differs: deleting a server-side session ends it at once. A signed token stays valid until it expires, so systems use short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus a refresh token that is checked against the server, or keep a deny list of revoked token ids.
Session ids must change at login (to prevent session fixation), expire after inactivity and after an absolute time, and be sent only over HTTPS in a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite set.

The Twelve-Factor App guidance says processes should be stateless and share nothing: anything that must persist goes to a backing service. That is what lets you add servers, restart them or replace them without logging users out.

useWhen: Server-side sessions for browser apps where logout and revocation must be immediate.
Short-lived signed tokens between services or for APIs where a lookup per request is expensive.
avoidWhen: Avoid storing sessions in one server’s memory in any setup with more than one server.
Avoid long-lived signed tokens without a revocation plan.

rows: Only a random id leaves the server
Waits for expiry or needs a deny list
Only an id leaves the server

numbers.title: What the session lookup costs
assumptions: 20,000 requests per second across the fleet (example)
A lookup in an in-memory key-value store takes about 0.5 ms on the local network (example)
Each lookup is a small read
steps: Added latency per request: about 0.5 ms.
Load on the store: 20,000 reads per second, well within what a single in-memory store node commonly handles (check your own benchmarks).
Caching the session inside each server for a few seconds would cut the reads but delay logout by up to those seconds.
Signed tokens remove the 20,000 reads but make immediate revocation need its own list.
numbers.result: Under these assumptions the lookup adds well under a millisecond per request; revocation, not speed, usually decides the design.

india.title: OWASP session management guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet recommends generating session ids with a cryptographically secure random generator, renewing the id after login, setting idle and absolute timeouts, and invalidating the session on the server at logout rather than only deleting the cookie in the browser. Deleting only the cookie leaves a copied id valid on the server, which is why server-side invalidation matters.

pitfalls.trap: “Stateless servers mean we have no session data.”
pitfalls.say: “The data is in a shared store or a signed token, so any server can serve the user.”

pitfalls.trap: “Signed tokens are better because they scale.”
pitfalls.say: “They save a lookup but complicate revocation; for a browser app needing instant logout I’d use server-side sessions.”

takeaways: HTTP forgets; a cookie or header must carry identity on every request.
Server-side sessions: random id, shared store, instant revocation.
Signed tokens: no lookup, but revocation needs expiry or a deny list.
Stateless servers keep no per-user data in their own memory.

interactive.title: What happens after a deploy?
interactive.prompt: Sessions are kept in each server’s memory. A deploy restarts all 4 servers one at a time.

choices.label: Users are logged out as their server restarts
choices.feedback: Right: in-memory sessions vanish with the process.

choices.label: Nothing: sessions are copied to the new servers
choices.feedback: Nothing copies in-memory data across a restart.

choices.label: Only users on the first server are affected
choices.feedback: Every server restarts, so every server’s users lose their sessions.

interactive.reveal: Move sessions to a shared store (or use signed tokens) so servers can restart, scale and be replaced without logging users out.

title: HTTP Methods and Status Codes
objectives: Use safe and idempotent methods correctly
Pick precise status codes for success, client errors and server errors
Tell 401 from 403 and 400 from 422

cards.title: Methods carry promises
cards.body: RFC 9110 defines what each method promises. Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change state. Idempotent methods (the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE) have the same effect whether sent once or many times. POST promises neither, and PATCH is not idempotent unless you design it to be.

cards.title: Misconception: 200 with an error message is fine
cards.body: Returning 200 OK with {"error": "not found"} hides failures from caches, monitoring, retries and client code that branch on status. Use the status code for the outcome and the body for details.

cards.title: Choosing a status, step by step
cards.body: Ask the questions in order and stop at the first match.
steps: Did the server fail? 5xx (500, 502, 503, 504)
Is the caller unauthenticated? 401; authenticated but not allowed? 403
Does the resource not exist? 404
Is the request malformed? 400; well-formed but invalid? 422; conflicting state? 409
Success: 200, 201 Created with a Location, or 204 No Content

cards.title: Redirects that keep the method
cards.body: 301 and 302 historically let clients change POST to GET on the redirect. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) require the same method and body; 303 See Other explicitly tells the client to follow with GET.

cards.title: Trap: changing state on GET
cards.body: A GET that deletes or updates something can be triggered by link prefetchers, crawlers and caches, which assume GET is safe. Use POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE for any change.

cards.title: Edge case: a 401 without WWW-Authenticate
cards.body: RFC 9110 requires a 401 response to include a WWW-Authenticate header naming how to authenticate (for example Bearer). APIs that omit it confuse generic clients and proxies. If the caller is authenticated but not allowed, the right code is 403; if you want to hide that a resource exists at all, 404 is a common deliberate choice.

questions.prompt: Which method is idempotent but not safe?

choices.label: GET
HEAD
PUT
POST

questions.explanation: PUT changes state, but repeating it leaves the same result.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user requests another customer’s invoice they are not allowed to see. Status?

choices.label: 403 Forbidden
400 Bad Request
500 Internal Server Error
401 Unauthorized

questions.explanation: 401 means not authenticated; this user is authenticated but not permitted (some APIs return 404 to hide existence).

questions.prompt: A request creates a new order. Best success response?

choices.label: 302 Found pointing to the order list
204 No Content
200 OK with an empty body
201 Created with a Location header for the new order

questions.explanation: 201 says something was created and Location says where.

questions.prompt: You permanently move a POST endpoint and clients must keep sending POST. Which status?

choices.label: 308 Permanent Redirect
301 Moved Permanently
303 See Other
302 Found

questions.explanation: 308 preserves the method and body; 303 switches to GET.

questions.prompt: Order the status classes by first digit.

items.label: 4xx client error
2xx success
5xx server error
1xx informational
3xx redirection

questions.explanation: The first digit gives the class.

questions.prompt: Sign-up with an email already registered.
constraints: Body is well-formed JSON
Clients show a specific message
The person signing up must be told the address is taken

approaches.label: 500 Internal Server Error
200 OK with {"error": "exists"}
409 Conflict with an error code in the body

rationaleOptions.label: The request conflicts with the current state of the resource
Clients and monitoring can branch on the status
500 is right because the insert failed

rationaleConflicts.r3: 5xx means the server failed; here the client asked for something that conflicts.

questions.explanation: Use 4xx for client-side problems and 5xx only when the server itself failed.

flashcards.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (and TRACE).
401: not authenticated. 403: authenticated but not allowed.
303 follows with GET; 307/308 keep the method and body.

mechanism.title: What HTTP semantics promise to every intermediary
steps: HTTP semantics are defined in RFC 9110. They matter because clients, proxies, caches, crawlers and retry logic all act on them without knowing your application. A cache may store a GET response; a client library may retry an idempotent request automatically after a network error.

Safe methods are read-only from the client’s point of view: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. Idempotent methods are the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE: sending one twice has the same intended effect as once. POST is neither; PATCH is neither by default.

Status codes are grouped by first digit. 2xx: success (200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted for work queued, 204 No Content). 3xx: redirection (301, 302, 303, 304 Not Modified, 307, 308). 4xx: the client must change something. 5xx: the server failed and the same request might work later.

Common client errors: 400 Bad Request (malformed), 401 Unauthorized (missing or bad credentials, sent with a WWW-Authenticate header), 403 Forbidden (known caller, not allowed), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Content (well-formed but invalid), 429 Too Many Requests.

Common server errors: 500 Internal Server Error (a bug), 502 Bad Gateway (an upstream gave a bad response), 503 Service Unavailable (overloaded or in maintenance, ideally with Retry-After), 504 Gateway Timeout (an upstream did not answer in time).
RFC 9457 defines “problem details”, a standard JSON body (type, title, status, detail) for error responses, so clients can show and log errors consistently.

useWhen: Use precise status codes so caches, clients and dashboards behave correctly without parsing bodies.
Use 202 Accepted for requests that start background work, with a URL to check status.
avoidWhen: Avoid 200 for errors and 500 for client mistakes; both distort error-rate monitoring.
Avoid GET for anything that changes state.

rows: Replace a resource at a known URL

numbers.title: Why status codes change your error rate
assumptions: 1,000,000 requests a day (example)
0.3% are validation failures, 0.05% are real server bugs (illustrative)
steps: Validation failures: 1,000,000 × 0.003 = 3,000 a day; server bugs: 1,000,000 × 0.0005 = 500 a day.
If validation failures return 500, the dashboard shows 3,500 server errors, 0.35%, and the 500 real bugs are hidden among them.
Returning 422 for validation failures leaves 500 server errors, 0.05%, a rate an alert can track.
An alert on “5xx above 0.1%” would fire constantly in the first design and only on real problems in the second.
numbers.result: Correct 4xx and 5xx codes keep the server error rate meaningful enough to alert on.

india.title: RFC 9110 and problem details
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9110, published in 2022, consolidated HTTP’s semantics (methods, status codes, headers) that were previously spread across several RFCs, and renamed 422 to “Unprocessable Content”. RFC 9457 (2023) defines the application/problem+json format for error bodies. Many public API style guides now point to these two documents rather than inventing their own conventions.

pitfalls.trap: “We return 200 for everything and put the status in the body.”
pitfalls.say: “That hides failures from caches, retries and monitoring; I’d use proper status codes and a problem-details body.”

pitfalls.trap: “401 and 403 are the same.”
pitfalls.say: “401 means we do not know who you are; 403 means we know and the answer is no.”

takeaways: Safe: no state change. Idempotent: same effect if repeated.
GET must never change state.
4xx: the client must change something; 5xx: the server failed.
401 is unauthenticated, 403 is forbidden; 307/308 keep the method.

interactive.title: Which status code?
interactive.prompt: A client sends well-formed JSON to create a booking, but the end date is before the start date.

choices.label: 422 Unprocessable Content
choices.feedback: Right: the syntax is fine, the content breaks a rule.

choices.label: 400 Bad Request
choices.feedback: Also acceptable in many APIs, but 422 is more specific for valid syntax with invalid content.

choices.label: 500 Internal Server Error
choices.feedback: Nothing failed on the server; the request is wrong.

interactive.reveal: Use 400 for malformed requests and 422 for well-formed requests that fail validation; keep 5xx for server failures so error rates stay meaningful.

title: Building Idempotent Endpoints
objectives: Make retries of a write harmless
Implement an idempotency-key store with its edge cases
Use natural idempotency where the operation allows it

cards.title: Retries are normal, duplicates are not
cards.body: Networks drop responses after the server has acted. The client cannot tell “never arrived” from “done, but the reply was lost”, so it retries. An idempotent endpoint makes the second attempt return the first result instead of acting twice.

cards.title: Misconception: a unique key on the table is enough
cards.body: A unique constraint stops a second row, but the second request then fails with an error, and the client cannot tell whether its payment went through. An idempotency key store records the first response and replays it, so the retry sees the same success.

cards.title: Handling a request with an idempotency key
cards.body: The key is chosen by the client, once per intended operation, and sent again on every retry.
steps: Look up the key: a stored response exists? Return it unchanged
Key in progress? Return 409 (or wait) so two copies do not run at once
New key: record it as in progress, with a hash of the request body
Do the work and store the response under the key with an expiry

cards.title: Natural idempotency
cards.body: Some operations can be made idempotent by their shape. “Set status to shipped” (a PUT of the final state) is safe to repeat; “add 1 to stock” is not. Conditional updates such as “set balance to 90 if version is 7” also repeat safely, because the second attempt finds version 8 and does nothing.

cards.title: Trap: same key, different body
cards.body: If a client reuses a key with a different amount, replaying the old response silently ignores the new request. Store a hash of the request with the key and reject a mismatch with an error.

cards.title: Edge case: key scope and key expiry
cards.body: Idempotency keys must be scoped to the caller (account or API key), or two clients that happen to pick the same key would receive each other’s stored results. Stored keys also expire, commonly after about a day; a retry that arrives after expiry is treated as new. Document the window, and keep retries well inside it.

questions.prompt: Why can a client not just avoid retrying writes?

choices.label: HTTP forbids timeouts on writes
It cannot tell a lost request from a lost response
Servers require at least two attempts
Retries are always faster than waiting

questions.explanation: A timeout leaves the outcome unknown; retrying is the only way to find out.

questions.prompt: Which of these request handlers is naturally idempotent?

choices.label: Set the order’s status to “shipped”
Append a line to the order history
Charge the card 500 rupees
Add 1 to the item’s stock count

questions.explanation: Setting a final value repeats safely; increments and appends do not.

questions.prompt: A retry arrives while the first request with the same key is still running. What should the server do?

choices.label: Run both in parallel and keep whichever finishes first
Reject or hold the second until the first finishes, then replay its result
Ignore the key and simply process it again
Delete the stored key and start the operation over

questions.explanation: Without an in-progress state, two copies of the operation can run at once.

questions.prompt: A client reuses an idempotency key with a different amount. Best response?

choices.label: Replay the original response
Charge the difference
An error saying the key was used with a different request
Process the new amount as a new payment

questions.explanation: Store a request hash with the key and reject mismatches.

questions.prompt: Order the server’s steps for a new idempotency key.

items.label: Check the key store
Return the response
Store the response under the key
Perform the operation
Record the key as in progress with a request hash

questions.explanation: Record the key before acting so concurrent retries see it.

questions.prompt: Making a “create payment” POST safe to retry.
constraints: Mobile clients retry on timeouts
Payments must never be duplicated
Clients need the same response on retry

approaches.label: Tell clients never to retry
Unique constraint on (user, amount, minute)
Client-generated idempotency key, stored with the response for 24 hours

rationaleOptions.label: The retry receives the original success response
A unique constraint on amount and minute identifies duplicates reliably
The key identifies the intended operation, not its content

rationaleConflicts.r3: Two genuine payments of the same amount in one minute would be wrongly blocked, and retries get an error.

questions.explanation: Idempotency keys identify the operation and let retries see the original result.

flashcards.front: What does an idempotency key identify?
flashcards.back: One intended operation, chosen by the client and reused on retries.
Unseen, in progress, completed (with the stored response).
Set-to-value (PUT of final state) and conditional updates.

mechanism.title: How an idempotency key store works
steps: The client generates a unique key (for example a random UUID) for each operation it intends to perform, such as “pay this invoice”, and sends it in a header on the first attempt and on every retry of that same operation.

The server keeps a table keyed by (client or account, key). Each record holds a state (in progress or completed), a hash of the request body, the stored response (status and body) and an expiry time such as 24 hours.

On arrival, the server tries to insert the key as in progress, using a unique constraint so that only one concurrent request can win the insert. The loser sees the existing record and either waits, returns 409 Conflict, or replays the stored response if it is complete.

The operation and the update of the key record should be atomic where possible, for example in the same database transaction. If the work involves an external call, such as a card network, record enough state to resume or to find out what happened before retrying it.
Expire keys after a window longer than any client would retry. Return an error if a key is reused with a different request body, because replaying the old response would hide a mistake.

Natural idempotency avoids the store entirely for some operations: PUT of a full state, DELETE of a known id, or conditional writes using a version number. Increments, appends and “create” operations need a key.

useWhen: Idempotency keys for create and charge operations that clients may retry.
Conditional writes with version numbers for updates that should apply once.
avoidWhen: Avoid deduplicating by business fields such as amount and time; real duplicates exist.
Avoid storing keys forever; set an expiry longer than the longest retry window.

rows: Creates with a natural unique field
Low, but retries look like failures

numbers.title: How many duplicates without idempotency
assumptions: 500,000 payment requests a day (illustrative)
0.2% of responses are lost or time out after the payment succeeded (illustrative)
Clients retry each of those once
steps: Lost responses after success: 500,000 × 0.002 = 1,000 a day.
Without idempotency each retry creates a second payment: 1,000 duplicate charges a day.
With a key store, those 1,000 retries replay the original response.
Storage: 500,000 keys a day kept for 24 hours, a few hundred bytes each, is on the order of a hundred megabytes.
numbers.result: A small loss rate at moderate volume still means about a thousand duplicates a day; a key store with a 24-hour expiry is cheap by comparison.

india.title: The IETF Idempotency-Key header draft
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The IETF HTTP APIs working group has a draft standard, “The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field”, that describes this pattern: the client sends a unique key with non-idempotent requests such as POST, the server stores the result, and repeated requests with the same key get the same result. It also describes error responses for a reused key with a different payload and for concurrent requests with the same key.

pitfalls.trap: “We use a unique constraint, so retries are safe.”
pitfalls.say: “The duplicate is blocked, but the retry gets an error; a key store replays the original success.”

pitfalls.trap: “POST can never be idempotent.”
pitfalls.say: “POST is not idempotent by definition, but an idempotency key makes a specific POST safe to retry.”

takeaways: Clients retry because a timeout hides the outcome.
A key store records in-progress and completed states and replays responses.
Reject a reused key with a different body.
Set-to-value and conditional writes are naturally idempotent.

interactive.title: What does the retry return?
interactive.prompt: A client sends “create payment of 500” with Idempotency-Key k1. The server charges the card and stores the 201 response, but the client times out and retries with the same key and body.

choices.label: The stored 201 response, without charging again
choices.feedback: Right: the key is completed, so the server replays the response.

choices.label: A second charge and a new 201
choices.feedback: That is what happens without a key store.

choices.label: A 409 error because the key exists
choices.feedback: 409 suits a key still in progress or a different body; a completed identical request gets the replay.

interactive.reveal: Completed keys replay; in-progress keys block a concurrent duplicate; mismatched bodies are rejected. That gives the client the same answer however many times it retries.

title: Authentication and Authorisation on the Server
objectives: Store passwords with a slow, salted hash
Check permissions on every request with least privilege
Avoid the common access-control bugs

cards.title: Who you are, then what you may do
cards.body: Authentication establishes identity: a password, a passkey, a one-time code or a token from an identity provider. Authorisation decides, on every request, whether that identity may perform this action on this resource.

cards.title: Misconception: hiding the button is access control
cards.body: Removing the “Delete” button from the page does nothing if the endpoint behind it still accepts the request. Every endpoint must check permissions on the server for the specific resource being touched.

cards.title: Checking a password
cards.body: The server never stores the password itself, only a slow hash of it with a per-user salt.
steps: Sign-up: generate a random salt; store salt and slow-hash(password, salt)
Login: load the user’s salt and hash
Compute slow-hash(entered password, salt)
Compare in constant time; on success start a session

cards.title: Roles, ownership and least privilege
cards.body: Role-based access control groups permissions into roles such as viewer, editor and admin. Most real rules also involve ownership (“may edit their own posts”). Grant each user and service the least privilege it needs, and deny by default.

cards.title: Trap: trusting the id in the URL
cards.body: Changing /invoices/1041 to /invoices/1042 must not show another customer’s invoice. This is the most common access-control bug: the code checks that the user is logged in but not that the record belongs to them.

cards.title: Edge case: bcrypt reads only 72 bytes
cards.body: bcrypt uses at most the first 72 bytes of its input, so two long passphrases that share their first 72 bytes produce the same hash, and multi-byte characters reach the limit sooner. Prefer Argon2id for new systems, or enforce a maximum length that fits. Never pre-hash with a fast hash and pass raw binary to bcrypt, because zero bytes can truncate the input.

questions.prompt: How should passwords be stored?

choices.label: Encrypted with a key kept on the same server
A slow, salted password hash such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt
Plain text in a separate table with strict access
A fast hash such as SHA-256 without a salt

questions.explanation: Slow, salted hashes make stolen hashes expensive to crack.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user requests /orders/88, which belongs to someone else. What must the server check?

choices.label: Only that the session is valid
That order 88 belongs to the user (or their role allows it)
That the request came from the app’s own page
That the id is a valid number

questions.explanation: Authentication alone does not grant access to every record.

questions.prompt: Which is an authorisation decision?

choices.label: Whether the one-time code is correct
Whether the passkey signature verifies
Whether the password matches
Whether this user may refund this order

questions.explanation: The others establish identity.

questions.prompt: Why add a unique salt per user?

choices.label: It lets the server decrypt the password when needed
It makes each hash faster to compute at login time
It removes the need for a slow hashing function
Equal passwords hash differently, defeating precomputed tables

questions.explanation: Salts defeat precomputed tables and reveal nothing about shared passwords.

questions.prompt: Order the checks for “refund order 88”.

items.label: Load order 88
Check the user may refund this order
Authenticate the session
Perform the refund
Write an audit log entry

questions.explanation: Identity, then the resource, then the permission on that resource.

questions.prompt: Permissions for an internal admin tool used by support staff.
constraints: Support may view orders and issue refunds up to a limit
Only finance may refund more
Auditors need a record

approaches.label: One shared admin account
Everyone is admin; trust staff
Roles with explicit permissions, a refund limit check, deny by default, and an audit log

rationaleOptions.label: Audit logs tie each action to a named person
A shared account is fine because the office is secure
Each person gets only the permissions their job needs

rationaleConflicts.r3: Shared accounts remove accountability and cannot be revoked per person.

questions.explanation: Least privilege, deny by default and per-person accounts with audit logs are the baseline.

flashcards.back: Who you are vs what you may do.
Slow salted hash (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt; PBKDF2 where required).
Not checking that the requested record belongs to the user.

mechanism.title: How a server verifies identity and enforces permissions
steps: Passwords are stored as the output of a deliberately slow, memory-hard hash function with a random per-user salt. OWASP’s current guidance lists Argon2id first, then scrypt, then bcrypt for legacy systems, and PBKDF2 where FIPS compliance is required. The cost settings are tuned so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second on the server.

A slow hash matters because stolen hashes are attacked offline. If one guess costs a microsecond, billions of guesses are cheap; if one guess costs tens of milliseconds and lots of memory, the same attack costs orders of magnitude more.

Login should give the same error for an unknown user and a wrong password, rate-limit attempts per account and per source, and offer a second factor. Comparing hashes uses a constant-time comparison to avoid timing leaks.

Authorisation runs on every request, on the server, for the specific resource. Typical models: role-based (permissions attached to roles), attribute-based (rules over user, resource and context attributes) and relationship-based (“members of this team may edit this document”).
Deny by default: an endpoint with no explicit rule should refuse access. Centralise checks in one place (middleware or a policy function) so new endpoints cannot forget them.
Record security-relevant actions (logins, permission changes, refunds) in an audit log with who, what, when and from where, and keep it where the people being audited cannot alter it.

useWhen: Centralised policy checks for every endpoint, with deny by default.
A modern slow hash with per-user salts for any stored password.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on the user interface to hide forbidden actions.
Avoid fast general-purpose hashes (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256) for passwords.

rows: Users may edit their own posts
Team members may edit team documents

numbers.title: Why slow hashing changes the attacker’s maths
assumptions: An attacker can try 10 billion fast hashes per second on rented hardware (illustrative)
A slow hash setting that allows only about 10,000 guesses per second on the same hardware (illustrative)
A list of 100 million candidate passwords
steps: Fast hash: 100,000,000 ÷ 10,000,000,000 = 0.01 s per user to try the whole list.
Slow hash: 100,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 10,000 s, about 2.8 hours per user.
With unique salts, that cost repeats for every user; no table can be reused.
For a million stolen accounts, the fast hash costs about 10,000 s (under three hours) in total, while the slow hash costs about 10,000 million seconds: over 300 years.
numbers.result: Slow, salted hashing multiplies the attacker’s cost per account by about a million in this example, which is the whole point.

india.title: OWASP’s top risk: broken access control
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In the OWASP Top 10 for 2021, “Broken Access Control” moved to the top position; OWASP reported that 94% of the applications in its data set were tested for some form of it, and it had more recorded occurrences than any other category. The typical examples are exactly this lesson’s trap: changing an id in a URL to view someone else’s record, and calling an endpoint the interface hides. OWASP’s guidance is to deny by default and enforce ownership checks on the server for every record.

pitfalls.trap: “We hash passwords with SHA-256, so they are safe.”
pitfalls.say: “SHA-256 is fast; I’d use Argon2id or bcrypt with a per-user salt so offline guessing is expensive.”

pitfalls.trap: “The admin pages are hidden, so normal users cannot reach them.”
pitfalls.say: “Hidden is not protected; every endpoint checks the caller’s permission on the server.”

takeaways: Authentication says who; authorisation decides what, on every request.
Store passwords with a slow, salted, memory-hard hash.
Check ownership of the specific record, not just login.
Deny by default, least privilege, audit sensitive actions.

interactive.title: Is this endpoint safe?
interactive.prompt: GET /api/invoices/{id} checks that the request has a valid session, then returns the invoice with that id.

choices.label: No: any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the id
choices.feedback: Right: it authenticates but never authorises the specific invoice.

choices.label: Yes: the session check stops strangers
choices.feedback: It stops anonymous users, not other customers.

choices.label: Yes, if invoice ids are large numbers
choices.feedback: Hard-to-guess ids reduce guessing but are not an access check.

interactive.reveal: Load the invoice and confirm it belongs to the caller (or that their role allows it) before returning it. Return 404 or 403 otherwise.

title: Concurrency: Processes, Threads and Async I/O
objectives: Compare process-per-request, thread pools and event loops
Size a thread pool with Little’s law
Spot blocking calls and shared-state races

cards.title: Three ways to serve many requests at once
cards.body: A server can run several processes, each with its own memory; several threads inside one process, sharing memory; or one event loop that starts many I/O operations and handles each as it completes. Most production servers combine them, for example one process per CPU core, each with threads or an event loop.

cards.title: Misconception: async makes code faster
cards.body: Asynchronous I/O lets one thread wait on thousands of slow network calls at once, which raises how many requests it can hold. It does not make any single CPU-bound computation faster, and one CPU-heavy callback blocks every other request on that loop.

cards.title: Sizing a thread pool, step by step
cards.body: Little’s law says the average number of requests in a system equals arrival rate × time each spends there.
steps: Measure: 400 requests per second
Each request holds a thread for 50 ms, mostly waiting on the database
Busy threads on average: 400 × 0.05 = 20
Add headroom for bursts and slow periods, for example a pool of about 40

cards.title: Shared state needs coordination
cards.body: Threads in one process share memory. Two threads incrementing the same counter can both read 5 and both write 6. Protect shared data with locks or atomic operations, or avoid sharing by giving each request its own data and keeping shared state in a database.

cards.title: Trap: a blocking call on the event loop
cards.body: An event-loop server runs every request’s callbacks on one thread. A single synchronous file read, CPU-heavy loop or blocking database driver call pauses all requests on that loop until it finishes. Move such work to a worker pool.

cards.title: Edge case: a pool that waits on itself
cards.body: A task running on a bounded thread pool that submits a sub-task to the same pool and waits for it can deadlock: once every thread is waiting for a sub-task, no thread is left to run any sub-task. It appears only under load. Use separate pools for dependent stages, or make the outer work asynchronous instead of blocking.

questions.prompt: A service receives 200 requests per second and each holds a thread for 100 ms. How many threads are busy on average?
Which workload gains most from an event loop with async I/O?

choices.label: Training a machine-learning model on one host
Resizing large images on the server CPU
Compressing uploaded video files in full
Thousands of mostly idle connections waiting on the network

questions.explanation: Async I/O helps with waiting; CPU-bound work needs more cores or workers.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run “read count, add 1, write count” at the same time, starting from 5. What can the final value be?

choices.label: Always 7
6 or 7, depending on how the steps interleave
An error, because threads cannot share memory
Always 6

questions.explanation: Without a lock or atomic increment, one update can be lost.

questions.prompt: Why do some servers run one process per CPU core?

choices.label: To avoid needing any network sockets
Because threads cannot run on more than one core
Because processes share memory more cheaply than threads
To use every core while keeping each process’s memory separate

questions.explanation: Processes isolate memory; one per core uses all cores.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to size a thread pool.

items.label: Add headroom for bursts
Multiply rate by time for the average busy threads
Measure how long each request holds a thread
Load-test and adjust
Measure the request rate

questions.explanation: Measure, apply Little’s law, add headroom, verify.

questions.prompt: An endpoint gets 1,500 requests per second and each request holds a thread for 40 ms. About how many threads are busy on average?
assumptions: 1,500 requests per second
40 ms per request
questions.explanation: Sanity check: if the database slows from 40 ms to 200 ms, the same traffic needs 300 busy threads, so pools sized for normal days run out exactly when a dependency gets slow; pair the pool with timeouts.

flashcards.back: Average in system = arrival rate × average time in system.
How many waiting requests one thread can hold, not CPU-bound speed.
Two read-modify-write sequences interleave; fix with locks or atomic operations.

sources.title: MDN: Event loop and concurrency model

mechanism.title: How each concurrency model spends its time
steps: Process-based servers fork or pre-start worker processes. Each has its own memory, so a crash or leak in one does not corrupt the others, but each also costs its own memory, and sharing data needs a database, cache or inter-process messaging.

Thread-based servers keep a pool of threads in one process; each request runs on one thread until it finishes. Blocking calls are simple to write, and a thread waiting on I/O does not use CPU, but every thread needs its own stack memory and the pool size caps concurrency.

Event-loop servers use a small number of threads and non-blocking I/O. A request starts an operation, registers what to do when it completes, and returns control; the loop handles completions as they arrive. This holds very many concurrent connections cheaply, as long as no callback blocks.

Little’s law (L = λ × W) connects them: the number of requests in progress equals the arrival rate times the time each spends in the system. A thread-per-request server needs at least that many threads; an event-loop server needs that many open operations, which is cheap.

Shared mutable state is where concurrency bugs live. A read-modify-write on shared memory needs a lock or an atomic operation; locks taken in different orders can deadlock. Many servers sidestep this by keeping request handling free of shared state and letting the database handle concurrency with transactions.
CPU-bound work does not benefit from more threads than cores. Run it in a separate worker pool sized to the cores, so it cannot starve the threads or loop serving I/O-bound requests.

useWhen: Event loops or many lightweight tasks for I/O-heavy services with many concurrent connections.
A bounded worker pool sized to cores for CPU-heavy work.
avoidWhen: Avoid unbounded thread pools; under a slow dependency they grow until memory runs out.
Avoid blocking calls inside an event loop.

numbers.title: What a slow database does to a thread pool
assumptions: 300 requests per second
Normal database latency 30 ms, so each request holds a thread for about 35 ms
Thread pool of 50
steps: Normal: 300 × 0.035 = 10.5 busy threads, comfortably inside 50.
Database slows to 300 ms: 300 × 0.305 ≈ 92 threads needed, but only 50 exist.
New requests queue for a thread, so latency climbs far beyond the 300 ms the database adds.
A 500 ms timeout on the query caps how long each request can hold a thread; shedding load or a circuit breaker protects the pool.
numbers.result: A tenfold slowdown in one dependency multiplies the threads needed tenfold; timeouts and load shedding keep the pool from exhausting.

india.title: Handling overload in the Google SRE book
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s chapter on handling overload describes how servers should reject excess work early rather than queue it without limit, because a long queue means every request waits and many time out anyway. It recommends limits on concurrent requests per server and per client, which is the practical form of sizing a pool with Little’s law and refusing work beyond it.

pitfalls.trap: “Switching to async will make the service faster.”
pitfalls.say: “It lets one thread hold more waiting requests; CPU-bound work and slow queries stay just as slow.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just make the thread pool bigger.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d size it with rate × time, add headroom, and protect it with timeouts; bigger pools just queue more work when a dependency slows.”

takeaways: Processes isolate memory; threads share it; event loops multiplex I/O on few threads.
Little’s law: in-flight = rate × time.
Shared mutable state needs locks or atomics.
Never block an event loop; size CPU pools to cores.

interactive.title: Size the thread pool
interactive.prompt: A service gets 400 requests per second and has a pool of 40 threads. Slide how long each request holds its thread (slow database days push this up) and find where the pool runs out.
interactive.takeaway: At 50 ms, 400 requests per second keep 20 threads busy, half the pool. At 100 ms all 40 are busy and requests start to queue. A slow dependency, not more traffic, is the usual way pools run out, which is why each call needs a timeout.

title: Background Jobs and Work Queues
objectives: Move slow work out of the request path
Make jobs safe to retry with at-least-once delivery
Schedule recurring work without running it twice

cards.title: Answer now, finish later
cards.body: Work that the user does not need to wait for (sending email, resizing images, generating a report) goes onto a queue. The request handler enqueues a job and responds quickly, often with 202 Accepted; worker processes take jobs from the queue and do them.

cards.title: Misconception: a job runs exactly once
cards.body: Most job queues deliver at least once. A worker can finish the work and crash before acknowledging it, and the queue will hand the job to another worker. Jobs must be idempotent: running twice must have the same effect as running once.

cards.title: A job from enqueue to done
cards.body: The acknowledgement comes last, so a crash means the job is retried rather than lost.
steps: Handler writes the job (and any data it needs) and returns 202
A worker claims the job; it becomes invisible to other workers for a lease time
Worker does the work idempotently
Worker acknowledges; the queue deletes the job
On failure: retry with backoff, then move to a dead-letter queue

cards.title: Retries and dead letters
cards.body: Transient failures (a timeout) deserve a retry with growing delays. Permanent failures (bad data) never succeed, so after a few attempts the job goes to a dead-letter queue for a person to inspect instead of blocking the queue forever.

cards.title: Trap: a cron job on every server
cards.body: Adding a scheduled task to each server’s scheduler runs it once per server. With five servers, the nightly invoice job runs five times. Use one scheduler that enqueues a job, or a lock that only one instance can take.

cards.title: Edge case: the job runs twice at the same time
cards.body: Queues that hide a taken job for a visibility timeout hand it to another worker if the first has not finished in time. A job that takes 90 s with a 60 s timeout is run twice concurrently, not just retried after a crash. Set the timeout above the slowest normal run, extend it while working, and make the job idempotent anyway.

questions.prompt: A sign-up handler sends a welcome email that takes 2 s. What should it do?

choices.label: Enqueue an email job and respond immediately
Ask the client to send the email itself
Skip the email when the server is busy
Send the email before responding

questions.explanation: The user does not need to wait for the email to be sent.

questions.prompt: Why must jobs be idempotent?

choices.label: Idempotent jobs use less memory on the workers
Queues always deliver every job exactly twice
Each worker runs every job on two threads at once
A job can be delivered again after a worker crashes before acknowledging

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible.

questions.prompt: A job fails because its input data is malformed. What should happen after a few attempts?

choices.label: Retry it forever with no delay
Delete it silently
Move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
Restart all workers

questions.explanation: Permanent failures need a person, not more retries.

questions.prompt: A nightly report is scheduled on each of 4 servers. What happens?

choices.label: It never runs because the servers conflict
It runs once, on the fastest server
It runs once and the others wait
The report runs 4 times

questions.explanation: Each scheduler fires independently.

questions.prompt: Order a job’s happy path.

items.label: Enqueue the job
Worker acknowledges
Worker claims it with a lease
Worker does the work
Queue deletes the job

questions.explanation: Acknowledge after the work so crashes cause a retry, not a loss.

questions.prompt: Sending invoice emails through a provider that sometimes times out.
constraints: Customers must get exactly one invoice email
Provider accepts a message id for deduplication
Outages last minutes

approaches.label: Send inline in the request and give up on error
Retry immediately in a tight loop until it works
Queue with retries and exponential backoff, a message id per invoice, and a dead-letter queue

rationaleOptions.label: The per-invoice message id stops duplicates when a retry follows a lost reply
Tight retry loops recover fastest
Backoff rides out short outages without hammering the provider

rationaleConflicts.r3: They pile load onto a struggling provider and can make the outage worse.

questions.explanation: Retry with backoff, deduplicate with a stable id, and park permanent failures.

flashcards.back: The work was queued, not finished; give a way to check status.
A job may run more than once, so it must be idempotent.
Where jobs go after repeated failure, for inspection.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Distributed Periodic Scheduling with Cron

mechanism.title: How a job queue keeps work from being lost or duplicated
steps: A queue stores jobs durably until a worker takes one. Common backings are a dedicated message broker, a database table used as a queue, or a managed queue service. The choice changes throughput and features, not the basic contract.

Claiming uses a lease (also called a visibility timeout): the job is hidden from other workers for a set time. If the worker acknowledges in time, the job is deleted; if it crashes or the lease runs out, the job becomes visible again and another worker takes it.

That contract gives at-least-once delivery. Exactly-once processing is achieved by making the job’s effects idempotent: check a “done” marker, use idempotency keys with external services, or write results with conditional updates.

Retries should back off exponentially with jitter and stop after a limit. Classify errors: transient ones (timeouts, 503) retry; permanent ones (validation errors, missing records) go straight to the dead-letter queue.

Scheduling recurring work needs one source of truth for “it is time”. Either a single scheduler process enqueues jobs, or every instance tries to take a lock (a database row or lease) and only the winner runs. The Google SRE book describes running such a scheduler with a leader elected among replicas.
Monitor queue depth and the age of the oldest job. Depth alone can be misleading; a small queue of very old jobs means workers are stuck.

useWhen: Queues for slow, retryable or bursty work that the user need not wait for.
A single scheduler or a lock for recurring jobs.
avoidWhen: Avoid queues for work whose result the user needs in the same response.
Avoid non-idempotent jobs; at-least-once delivery will eventually duplicate them.

rows: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

numbers.title: Workers needed for a burst
assumptions: A sale sends 12,000 email jobs in 10 minutes (illustrative)
Each job takes 0.5 s of worker time
Goal: clear the burst within about 15 minutes
steps: Total work: 12,000 × 0.5 s = 6,000 worker-seconds.
Within 15 minutes (900 s): 6,000 ÷ 900 ≈ 6.7, so about 7 workers.
With 3 workers it takes 6,000 ÷ 3 = 2,000 s, about 33 minutes.
Watching the oldest job’s age shows whether the target is being met.
numbers.result: Divide total work by the time allowed to get the worker count; the queue absorbs the burst meanwhile.

india.title: Distributed cron at Google
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book chapter “Distributed Periodic Scheduling with Cron” describes how running cron on individual machines failed at scale, because jobs ran twice or not at all when machines were added or failed. Its design runs the scheduler as a replicated service with one leader and records the state of each launch so that a failover does not launch a job twice. That is the large-scale form of “one scheduler, or a lock”.

pitfalls.trap: “The queue guarantees each job runs once.”
pitfalls.say: “Most queues are at-least-once; I’d make jobs idempotent so duplicates are harmless.”

pitfalls.trap: “Put the nightly job in cron on each server.”
pitfalls.say: “That runs it once per server; I’d use one scheduler or a lock so it runs once.”

takeaways: Queue slow work and respond with 202.
Leases plus acknowledgements give at-least-once delivery; make jobs idempotent.
Retry transient errors with backoff; dead-letter permanent ones.
Run scheduled jobs from one scheduler or behind a lock.

interactive.title: Why did the customer get two emails?
interactive.prompt: A worker sends a confirmation email, then crashes before acknowledging the job. A minute later, the customer receives a second identical email.

choices.label: The lease expired and the job was redelivered to another worker
choices.feedback: Right: that is at-least-once delivery working as designed.

choices.label: The queue always sends every job twice
choices.feedback: Duplicates come from crashes and timeouts, not from every job.

choices.label: The email provider duplicated it
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but the crash before acknowledgement explains it.

interactive.reveal: Make the job idempotent: record “email sent for order 42” before or atomically with sending, or pass a stable message id the provider deduplicates on.

title: Configuration and the Twelve-Factor App
objectives: Separate configuration from code
Keep secrets out of the repository and logs
Apply the twelve-factor ideas that matter most for servers

cards.title: One build, many environments
cards.body: The same build should run in development, staging and production. What differs between them (database addresses, credentials, feature switches, external service URLs) is configuration, and it should be supplied at deploy time, not baked into the code.

cards.title: Misconception: a private repository is a safe place for secrets
cards.body: Secrets in a repository spread to every clone, every laptop, every continuous integration log and the full history, where deleting the file does not remove them. Keep secrets in a secret manager or the deployment platform, inject them at runtime, and rotate any that were ever committed.

cards.title: Where a setting comes from at startup
cards.body: Read configuration once at startup, validate it, and fail fast if anything required is missing.
steps: Defaults in code for harmless settings (page size 20)
Environment-specific values supplied by the deploy (database URL)
Secrets fetched from the secret store or injected by the platform
Validate types and required keys; refuse to start if invalid

cards.title: The factors that matter most
cards.body: Of the twelve, a few prevent the most outages: config in the environment, backing services treated as attached resources, stateless share-nothing processes, fast startup and graceful shutdown, logs written as an event stream to standard output, and development kept close to production.

cards.title: Trap: printing the config at startup
cards.body: Logging “starting with config: …” is handy until it includes the database password and the logs ship to a third-party service. Log which keys were set, never their secret values.

cards.title: Failure story: an old flag reused in a partial deploy
cards.body: Publicly reported (US SEC order, 2013): on 1 August 2012 Knight Capital deployed new trading code to only seven of its eight servers, and reused a configuration flag that on the eighth server still switched on old, unused code. That code sent millions of unintended orders in about 45 minutes and the firm lost more than $460 million. Lessons: never repurpose flags, verify every instance runs the same build, and have a fast way to switch a feature off.

questions.prompt: Which value is configuration rather than code?

choices.label: The function that calculates tax
The validation rules for a sign-up form
The production database host name
The order of middleware in the request pipeline

questions.explanation: It varies between deploys of the same build.

questions.prompt: A database password was committed to Git last month and deleted today. What must happen?

choices.label: Nothing: it was deleted from the latest commit
Make the repository private from now on
Rotate the password; it is still in the history and clones
Rename the variable that used to hold it

questions.explanation: Deleting from the latest commit leaves it in history.

questions.prompt: What does twelve-factor say about logs?

choices.label: Each process manages its own rotating log files
Send each log line directly to an email inbox
Log only errors, to save as much disk space as possible
Write them as an event stream to standard output for the platform

questions.explanation: The environment captures and routes the stream.

questions.prompt: A required setting is missing at startup. What should the service do?

choices.label: Guess a sensible default silently
Retry reading it forever
Refuse to start, with a clear message naming the setting
Start and fail on the first request that needs it

questions.explanation: Failing fast surfaces the problem at deploy time, not under traffic.

questions.prompt: Order how a service loads configuration.

items.label: Validate types and required keys
Start serving traffic
Read environment-specific values
Apply defaults from code
Load secrets from the secret store

questions.explanation: Assemble, validate, then serve.

questions.prompt: Supplying an API key for a payment provider to a service in production.
constraints: Several engineers deploy
Key must be rotatable without a code change
Auditors ask who can read it

approaches.label: Hard-code it in a constants file
Commit an encrypted file with the key next to the code
Store it in a secret manager and inject it at runtime

rationaleOptions.label: Rotation is a change in the secret store, not a deploy
Encrypted files in the repo are as good as a secret manager
Access to read the secret can be restricted and logged

rationaleConflicts.r3: The decryption key still has to be distributed, and rotation needs a commit.

questions.explanation: Secrets live in a secret store, are injected at runtime and can be rotated and audited.

flashcards.back: Could the codebase be open-sourced now without exposing credentials? (twelve-factor’s test)
Rotate it; history keeps it.
Fail fast at startup.

mechanism.title: How configuration and secrets reach a running service
steps: The Twelve-Factor App, a methodology published by engineers at Heroku, defines config as everything likely to vary between deploys: resource handles, credentials and per-deploy values. It recommends storing config in environment variables, which are language- and OS-agnostic and hard to commit by accident.
Its litmus test: could the codebase be made open source at any moment without compromising credentials? If not, config and secrets are mixed into code.

Secrets deserve more than plain environment variables in many setups. A secret manager stores them encrypted, controls who and what can read each secret, logs access, and supports rotation. The platform injects them as files or environment variables at runtime.

Load configuration once at startup into a typed structure, validate it (required keys, formats, ranges) and refuse to start if it is invalid. A service that starts with a missing setting fails later, under traffic, in a harder-to-debug way.

Other factors complement this. Backing services (databases, caches, queues) are attached resources addressed by config, so swapping one is a config change. Processes are stateless and disposable: quick to start, shutting down gracefully on a termination signal by finishing in-flight requests.
Feature flags are a special kind of runtime config that change behaviour without a deploy; they need owners and expiry dates so they do not accumulate.

useWhen: Environment-supplied config and a secret manager for any service deployed to more than one environment.
Startup validation that names missing or invalid settings.
avoidWhen: Avoid committing secrets, even to private repositories or in “example” files.
Avoid environment-specific branches in code such as “if production then …”.

rows: Visible to child processes and some diagnostics

numbers.title: The cost of a secret in Git history
assumptions: A repository has 40 contributors and 25 CI runners with clones (illustrative)
A secret was committed 30 days ago
steps: Copies of the secret: at least 40 + 25 = 65 clones, plus any forks and backups.
Deleting the file creates a new commit; all 65 copies keep the old one.
Rewriting history needs every clone to be replaced, which is rarely complete.
Rotating the secret makes every copy worthless in one step.
numbers.result: Once committed, a secret has dozens of copies; rotation is the only fix that reaches all of them.

india.title: The Twelve-Factor App methodology
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Twelve-Factor App (12factor.net) was written in 2011 from experience running many applications on Heroku’s platform. Its twelve factors (codebase, dependencies, config, backing services, build-release-run, processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs and admin processes) have become a common vocabulary for deployable services. Container platforms follow many of them directly, for example by injecting config as environment variables and collecting logs from standard output.

pitfalls.trap: “It is a private repo, so the keys are fine there.”
pitfalls.say: “Every clone and CI log has them; I’d move them to a secret manager and rotate them.”

pitfalls.trap: “We check if it is production in the code.”
pitfalls.say: “Behaviour should differ by config, not by environment checks in code, so the same build runs everywhere.”

takeaways: Config varies between deploys; code does not.
Secrets go in a secret manager, injected at runtime, rotatable.
Validate config at startup and fail fast.
Stateless, disposable processes and logs to standard output.

interactive.title: What is the real risk?
interactive.prompt: A developer adds a debug line that prints the full configuration at startup. Logs are shipped to a hosted log service that 30 people can search.

choices.label: The database password is now readable by everyone with log access
choices.feedback: Right: logs are copied and retained widely; secrets must never be printed.

choices.label: Startup becomes noticeably slower
choices.feedback: One log line costs microseconds; exposure is the problem.

choices.label: Nothing, because the log service is private
choices.feedback: Private to 30 people and its own retention, which is far wider than the secret’s intended audience.

interactive.reveal: Log which settings are present (and non-secret values), never secret values. Treat any secret that reached logs as exposed and rotate it.
