title: Logging and Metrics for Services
objectives: Write structured logs with the right level and context
Choose metrics for rate, errors and duration
Read latency percentiles instead of averages

cards.title: Logs tell stories, metrics count
cards.body: A log line records one event with its details: this request, this user, this error. A metric is a number aggregated over time: requests per second, errors per minute, the 99th-percentile latency. Logs answer “what happened to this request?”; metrics answer “is the service healthy?”.

cards.title: Misconception: the average latency describes users
cards.body: An average of 120 ms can hide that 1 in 100 requests takes 3 seconds. Percentiles show the tail: p50 is the median, p99 is the value 99% of requests beat. Users who make many requests per page are likely to hit the tail.

cards.title: One useful log line
cards.body: Structured logs are key-value records that machines can filter and humans can read.
steps: Timestamp in UTC and a level (info, warn, error)
Request id and the service name
What happened: “payment declined”
Context as fields: order id, amount, provider, duration_ms
No secrets or full personal data

cards.title: The signals to watch
cards.body: For every request-serving service, track rate (requests per second), errors (failed requests per second or as a fraction) and duration (latency percentiles). Add saturation, such as CPU, memory, pool usage or queue depth, to see trouble coming.

cards.title: Trap: a metric label per user
cards.body: Labelling a metric with user id or request id creates one time series per value. Millions of users means millions of series, which can overload the metrics system. Put high-cardinality details in logs or traces, and keep metric labels to small sets such as endpoint and status class.

cards.title: Edge case: averaging percentiles
cards.body: The p99 of a fleet is not the average of each server’s p99. One overloaded server with p99 of 3 s and nine healthy ones at 200 ms average to 480 ms, hiding that a tenth of users wait seconds. Aggregate raw histograms (bucket counts) across servers and compute the percentile from the merged data.

questions.prompt: Which question do metrics answer better than logs?

choices.label: Is the error rate higher than usual right now?
Why did order 8812 fail?
What did the payment provider reply for this request?
Which user changed this setting yesterday?

questions.explanation: Aggregates over time are what metrics are for.

questions.prompt: p99 latency is 2 s and p50 is 80 ms. What does that mean?

choices.label: Most requests are slow, and a few are fast
The average request takes about 2 seconds
1% of requests take 2 s or longer, while half take 80 ms or less
Exactly 99 requests in total took 2 seconds

questions.explanation: Percentiles describe the distribution, including the tail.

questions.prompt: Which log line is most useful?

choices.label: error in handler at line 212 of the payment module
payment failed!!! please check the logs for details
level=error msg="payment declined" request_id=ab12 order_id=88 provider=bankx
ERROR something went wrong while handling the request

questions.explanation: Fields let you search by request, order or provider.

questions.prompt: Which metric label is safe to add?

choices.label: HTTP status class (2xx, 4xx, 5xx)
Request id
Full request URL with query string
User id

questions.explanation: Small, bounded label sets keep the number of time series manageable.

questions.prompt: Order an investigation of a latency alert.

items.label: Read the details of one slow request
Alert fires on p99 latency
Search logs or traces for slow request ids
Check rate, errors and saturation dashboards
Find the slow endpoint by its metric label

questions.explanation: Metrics narrow it down; logs and traces explain one case.

questions.prompt: A page makes 20 independent backend requests, each with a 1% chance of being slower than p99. About what percentage of page loads hit at least one slow request?
assumptions: 20 requests per page
1% chance each, independent
questions.explanation: Design implication: a tail that looks rare per request touches almost one page load in five, so pages that fan out need p99 targets, not just healthy medians.

flashcards.back: Logs: individual events with detail. Metrics: numbers aggregated over time.
Averages hide the tail; p95/p99 show it.
Avoid on metrics; keep ids in logs and traces.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How logs, metrics and traces fit together
steps: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events. Structured logs (for example JSON with consistent field names) can be filtered by any field. Levels separate routine events (info) from things that need attention (warn, error).

Metrics are numeric time series: counters that only go up (requests served), gauges that go up and down (queue depth) and histograms that record distributions (latency), from which percentiles are calculated.

Traces follow one request across services as a tree of spans, each with a start, a duration and attributes. The request id (trace id) links logs, spans and the user’s complaint together. OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral standards for all three signals.

The Google SRE book names four golden signals for user-facing systems: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Measure latency for successful and failed requests separately, because fast errors can make latency look better than it is.
Percentiles must be computed from distributions, not averaged. The p99 of a service is not the average of each server’s p99; aggregate histograms, then compute the percentile.

Logs need care: keep secrets, tokens and full personal data out of them, sample very high-volume debug logs, and set retention. Metric labels must have bounded values to keep the number of time series under control.

useWhen: Metrics with alerts on rate, errors, latency percentiles and saturation for every service.
Structured logs with a request id on every line, plus traces across service boundaries.
avoidWhen: Avoid alerting on averages; alert on percentiles or error ratios against an objective.
Avoid user ids, request ids or raw URLs as metric labels.

numbers.title: How big is the log bill?
assumptions: 3,000 requests per second (example)
Each request writes 4 log lines of about 300 bytes
steps: Per second: 3,000 requests × 1,200 bytes (4 lines of 300) = 3.6 MB.
Keeping 30 days: about 9.3 TB before compression.
Cutting debug lines to one in a hundred requests, or logging one line per request, divides this several times over.
numbers.result: Ordinary-looking logging at a few thousand requests per second is hundreds of gigabytes a day; decide per line whether it earns its cost.

india.title: The four golden signals
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In the Google SRE book chapter “Monitoring Distributed Systems”, the four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation, with the advice that if you can measure only four metrics of a user-facing system, these are the ones. The chapter also warns against averages for latency and recommends histograms and percentiles, and it argues that pages should be rare and actionable, not triggered by every small blip.

pitfalls.trap: “Average latency is 120 ms, so users are fine.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d look at p95 and p99; a page with 20 calls hits the tail on many loads.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add the user id as a metric label so we can filter.”
pitfalls.say: “That creates a series per user; I’d keep user ids in logs and traces and keep metric labels bounded.”

takeaways: Logs explain single events; metrics track health over time; traces follow a request.
Use structured logs with a request id; never log secrets.
Watch rate, errors, duration and saturation.
Percentiles, not averages; bounded metric labels.

interactive.title: Is the service healthy?
interactive.prompt: Dashboard: average latency 110 ms (normal), p50 90 ms (normal), p99 4.2 s (normally 400 ms), error rate normal.

choices.label: No: a slice of requests is very slow, and the average hides it
choices.feedback: Right: p99 went up tenfold while the average barely moved.

choices.label: Yes: the average and median are normal
choices.feedback: They describe typical requests, not the slow tail users notice.

choices.label: Cannot tell without the error rate rising
choices.feedback: Slow successes are a problem even without errors.

interactive.reveal: Tail latency often comes from one dependency, one shard or one kind of request. Break p99 down by endpoint and find slow request ids in traces or logs.

title: Error Handling and Retries
objectives: Classify errors as retryable or not
Retry with exponential backoff, jitter and a budget
Return errors that help callers without leaking internals

cards.title: Not every error deserves a retry
cards.body: A timeout or a 503 may succeed if tried again later. A 400 or a 404 will fail the same way every time. Retrying only the transient kind avoids hammering a service with requests that can never work.

cards.title: Misconception: retrying immediately recovers fastest
cards.body: When a service is overloaded, instant retries from every client multiply its load just when it can least take it. Waiting longer after each failure (exponential backoff) and adding randomness (jitter) spreads the retries out so the service can recover.

cards.title: A retry policy, step by step
cards.body: Each rule stops a different way retries make outages worse.
steps: Retry only transient errors, and only idempotent or keyed requests
Wait base × 2^attempt, capped (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms …)
Randomise each wait (jitter) so clients do not retry in lockstep
Stop after a few attempts or when the caller’s deadline is near
Honour Retry-After when the server sends it

cards.title: Errors callers can act on
cards.body: Return a status that says whose problem it is, a stable machine-readable error code, and a human-readable message. Log the stack trace with the request id on the server, but do not send stack traces or SQL errors to clients.

cards.title: Trap: retries at every layer
cards.body: If the app makes up to 3 attempts, the service it calls makes up to 3, and the database client makes up to 3, one user request can become 3³ = 27 database attempts during an outage. (Counted as “3 retries” after a first try, it is 4³ = 64.) Retry at one layer, usually the one closest to the user, and let inner layers fail fast.

cards.title: Edge case: retrying after a timeout
cards.body: A timeout does not tell you whether the server did the work. Retrying a payment or order creation after a timeout can do it twice unless the request carries an idempotency key. Retry freely only for idempotent methods, or for writes the server deduplicates. Retry-After may be either a number of seconds or an HTTP date, so parse both.

questions.prompt: Which failure is worth retrying?

choices.label: 400 Bad Request with a missing field
503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 2
404 Not Found for a deleted order
422 Unprocessable Content for a bad date

questions.explanation: Only transient failures can succeed on a later attempt.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to backoff?

choices.label: To make the total time spent retrying shorter
To make each retry faster
So many clients do not retry at the same instants
To guarantee the retry succeeds

questions.explanation: Synchronised retries create load spikes; randomness spreads them.

questions.prompt: A gateway, a service and a client library each retry up to 3 tries in total. When the data store is down, how many attempts can it receive from one click?
What should a 500 response body contain for an external client?

choices.label: A generic message, an error code and the request id
The server’s configuration and environment
The full stack trace from the exception
The failing SQL statement and its parameters

questions.explanation: Details stay in server logs, found via the request id.

questions.prompt: Order a well-behaved retry.

items.label: Wait an exponentially growing, jittered delay
Check the error is retryable and the request is safe to repeat
Give up and report after the attempt limit
Retry if the deadline allows
Request fails with a transient error

questions.explanation: Classify, wait, retry within limits, then stop.

questions.prompt: Retry policy for a checkout service calling an inventory service.
constraints: Inventory sometimes returns 503 for a few seconds
Checkout has a 2 s deadline
Inventory calls are idempotent

approaches.label: Up to 2 retries with jittered exponential backoff, within the deadline, at the checkout layer only
Retry at checkout, inventory and the database client
Retry immediately up to 10 times

rationaleOptions.label: One retrying layer keeps amplification predictable
Bounded, spread-out retries ride out short blips without piling on load
More layers retrying means more resilience

rationaleConflicts.r3: Retries multiply across layers and overload the struggling service.

questions.explanation: Retry a little, at one layer, with backoff and jitter, within the deadline.

flashcards.back: Timeouts, connection resets, 429/503 (honour Retry-After), sometimes 502/504.
Wait base × 2^n (capped), randomised, between attempts.
Attempts at several layers multiply: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers gives 3³ = 27.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures
RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

mechanism.title: How a service should fail and how callers should retry
steps: Classify each error by cause. Client errors (most 4xx) mean the request must change. Server errors and network failures may be transient. Some 4xx are transient too: 429 Too Many Requests means “slow down and try later”, and 408 Request Timeout may succeed on retry.
Only retry requests that are safe to repeat: idempotent methods, or non-idempotent requests carrying an idempotency key. Retrying a non-idempotent POST without one can duplicate the action.

Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt up to a cap. Jitter randomises each wait, for example choosing uniformly between zero and the backoff value, so thousands of clients that failed together do not all retry at the same moment.

Retry budgets bound the extra load: limit attempts per request, and limit retries to a fraction of total traffic (the Google SRE book suggests per-client retry budgets, such as retries being at most 10% of requests). Stop retrying when the caller’s deadline cannot be met.

When a service is overloaded it should say so cheaply: return 503 or 429 quickly, with Retry-After where possible, instead of accepting work it cannot finish. Fast failure is easier to retry and easier to recover from than slow timeouts.

Error responses should follow one shape across the API, for example RFC 9457 problem details, with a stable error type, a short title and the request id. Internal details (stack traces, query text, host names) go to logs only.

useWhen: Backoff with jitter and a small attempt limit for transient errors on safe-to-repeat requests.
One retrying layer, with inner layers failing fast.
avoidWhen: Avoid retrying 4xx errors such as 400 and 404.
Avoid unbounded retries or retries that ignore the caller’s deadline.

numbers.title: Total waiting with exponential backoff
assumptions: Base delay 200 ms, doubling each attempt, cap 5 s (example policy)
Up to 5 retries
steps: Maximum waits before each retry: 200, 400, 800, 1,600, 3,200 ms.
With full jitter each wait is random between 0 and that value, about 3.1 s in total on average.
If the caller’s deadline is 2 s, at most the first three retries (200 + 400 + 800 = 1,400 ms of waiting) can fit, so a policy of 5 retries is wasted here.
numbers.result: Add up the waits before choosing an attempt limit; the deadline, not hope, sets how many retries make sense.

india.title: Retries and cascading failures in the SRE book
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s chapter on cascading failures describes how retries amplify overload, gives the example of retries at multiple layers multiplying load, and recommends randomised exponential backoff, per-request retry limits, a server-wide retry budget and retrying at only one layer of the stack. It also recommends separate error codes for “overloaded, do not retry” so that clients stop adding load.

pitfalls.trap: “We retry everything three times to be safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Retrying 4xx never helps and retrying at every layer multiplies load; I’d retry transient errors at one layer with jittered backoff.”

pitfalls.trap: “Return the stack trace so clients can debug.”
pitfalls.say: “Clients get an error code and request id; the stack trace stays in our logs.”

takeaways: Retry transient errors only, and only safe-to-repeat requests.
Exponential backoff with jitter, capped, within the deadline.
Retry at one layer; inner layers fail fast.
Consistent error bodies with codes and request ids; no internals.

interactive.title: Add up the backoff
interactive.prompt: A client retries a failing call with a 200 ms base delay that doubles each time, capped at 5 s, and the caller gives up after 2 s. Slide the number of retries and see the longest wait and the total time spent waiting.
interactive.takeaway: Waits double: 200, 400, 800, 1,600 ms. Three retries add up to 1,400 ms of waiting and fit the 2 s deadline; a fourth brings the total to 3,000 ms, after the caller has already given up. Pick the attempt limit from the caller’s deadline; jitter then randomises each wait below these maximums.

title: Evolving and Versioning APIs
objectives: Tell compatible changes from breaking ones
Compare URL, header and media-type versioning
Retire an old version without stranding clients

cards.title: Most changes need no new version
cards.body: Adding an optional field to a response, a new endpoint or an optional request parameter is backward compatible: existing clients keep working. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type or meaning, or making an optional input required breaks them.

cards.title: Misconception: clients ignore fields they do not know
cards.body: Many do, but some validate responses strictly or map them into fixed structures, and enums are a common trap: a new status value such as “partially_refunded” can crash a client that only expected three values. Document that clients must tolerate unknown fields and values, and treat new enum values with care.

cards.title: Retiring a version, step by step
cards.body: Old versions should end on a published schedule, with signals in the responses themselves.
steps: Release v2 alongside v1; document the differences
Mark v1 deprecated; send Deprecation and Sunset headers with a date
Measure who still calls v1 and contact them
After the sunset date, return 410 Gone with a link to the migration guide

cards.title: Where the version goes
cards.body: A version in the URL path (/v2/orders) is visible and easy to route and cache. A version in a header or media type keeps URLs stable but is easier to forget. Whatever you choose, use it consistently and version the whole API rather than individual fields.

cards.title: Trap: a new version for every change
cards.body: Shipping v3, v4 and v5 within a year multiplies the code paths you must keep alive and confuses clients. Prefer additive, compatible changes, and save new major versions for changes that truly cannot be made compatibly.

cards.title: Edge case: additive changes that still break clients
cards.body: Adding a field is safe only if clients ignore unknown fields. Strict schema validators and generated clients that reject unknown properties fail on the new field. Publish a compatibility policy (“clients must ignore unknown fields and enum values”), test against old client versions, and treat any change to defaults as breaking.

questions.prompt: Which change is backward compatible for existing clients?

choices.label: Renaming “total” to “amount”
Changing “price” from a number to a string
Making an optional request field required
Adding an optional field to the response

questions.explanation: Additions that nobody must send or read are safe.

questions.prompt: What should v1 return after its announced sunset date?

choices.label: 410 Gone with a link to the migration guide
200 with the old behaviour, silently
500 Internal Server Error
301 to the v2 endpoint for every request

questions.explanation: 410 says the resource is intentionally gone; a blind redirect can change meaning.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of putting the version in the URL path?

choices.label: It is visible in logs and easy to route and cache
It allows a different version per field
Clients cannot forget to send it
URLs never change between versions

questions.explanation: A path version shows up in every log line and is easy to route and cache. It applies to the whole URL, not to single fields; clients can still call the wrong version; and the URLs do change between versions.

questions.prompt: Adding a new value to a status enum is risky because…

choices.label: servers must send every value twice
enums cannot be changed in any API
clients with a fixed list of values may fail on the new one
old clients will start sending the new value

questions.explanation: Tell clients to handle unknown values, and announce new ones.

questions.prompt: Order the retirement of an API version.

items.label: Return 410 Gone after the sunset date
Send deprecation headers and track remaining callers
Contact the remaining callers
Announce deprecation with a sunset date
Release the new version alongside the old

questions.explanation: Overlap, announce, measure, then remove.

questions.prompt: Splitting “name” into “first_name” and “last_name” in a public API.
constraints: Hundreds of client apps in the wild
Some clients update rarely
New clients want the split fields

approaches.label: Release v2 just for this field
Add the new fields and keep “name” for now, deprecated
Replace “name” in place

rationaleOptions.label: Old clients keep reading “name” unchanged
Clients will update within a week of the release
No new version to run in parallel for a single field

rationaleConflicts.r3: Public clients, especially mobile apps, can run old versions for months.

questions.explanation: Prefer additive changes plus deprecation over a new major version.

flashcards.back: Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meaning, making inputs required.
Deprecation and Sunset headers, docs, then 410 Gone.
Evolve compatibly; new major versions only when unavoidable.

sources.title: RFC 8594: The Sunset HTTP Header Field
RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field

mechanism.title: How APIs change without breaking their clients
steps: A change is backward compatible if every existing client keeps working without modification. Additions are usually compatible: new endpoints, new optional request fields, new response fields. Changes and removals usually are not.

Compatibility depends on client behaviour, so publish the rules: clients must ignore unknown fields, must handle unknown enum values (for example by treating them as “other”), and must not depend on field order. Servers in turn must keep accepting what they accepted before.

When a breaking change is unavoidable, introduce a new major version and run it alongside the old one. Common placements: the URL path (/v2/), a custom request header, or the media type in Accept (application/vnd.example.v2+json). Date-based versions pinned per client account are another approach some public APIs use.

Run versions side by side by translating at the edge where possible: the newest version is implemented once, and adapters convert older request and response shapes. This keeps old versions cheap to maintain until they are removed.

Deprecation is a process with signals. RFC 9745 defines a Deprecation response header and RFC 8594 a Sunset header carrying the date after which the resource will stop responding. Track calls per version and per client to know who must migrate.
After the sunset, return 410 Gone (or 404) with a link to the migration guide rather than silently changing behaviour.

useWhen: Additive changes plus clear tolerance rules for clients.
A new major version, with an announced overlap period, for unavoidable breaking changes.
avoidWhen: Avoid per-field or per-endpoint version numbers that multiply combinations.
Avoid removing an old version without measuring who still uses it.

numbers.title: How long an old version lingers
assumptions: A mobile app has 1 million monthly active users (illustrative)
Each month 30% of the users still on the old app version update (illustrative)
steps: After 1 month: 1,000,000 × 0.7 = 700,000 still on the old version.
An API version used by that app must stay up for many months, or those users break.
numbers.result: Under this illustrative update rate, a meaningful number of users stay on an old client for a year, so public API versions need long overlaps.

india.title: Deprecation and Sunset headers
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 8594 (2019) defines the Sunset header, an HTTP date after which a resource is expected to become unresponsive, and RFC 9745 (2025) defines the Deprecation header, signalling that a resource is or will be deprecated, optionally with a link to documentation. Both give clients a machine-readable warning in every response, so client teams can find deprecated calls through their own monitoring instead of waiting for an email.

pitfalls.trap: “We will just ship v2 and turn off v1 next month.”
pitfalls.say: “Mobile and partner clients update slowly; I’d run both, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, measure callers and then retire v1.”

pitfalls.trap: “Adding a field is always safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Usually, if clients ignore unknown fields; new enum values and stricter validation can still break clients.”

takeaways: Additions are compatible; removals, renames and type changes break.
Publish client rules: ignore unknown fields and values.
Major versions only for unavoidable breaks, run side by side.
Deprecate with headers and dates, measure, then return 410.

interactive.title: Will old clients break?
interactive.prompt: You add a new value “on_hold” to an order status that used to be one of “pending”, “shipped” or “delivered”. A popular client app maps the status into a fixed list and fails on unknown values.

choices.label: Yes: that client fails on orders with the new status
choices.feedback: Right: adding an enum value is only compatible for clients that tolerate unknown values.

choices.label: No: adding values is always backward compatible
choices.feedback: Adding fields is usually safe; adding enum values depends on client behaviour.

choices.label: No: the client will treat it as “pending”
choices.feedback: Only if it was written to fall back; this one fails.

interactive.reveal: Treat new enum values as a potentially breaking change: announce them, document “handle unknown values”, and consider sending them only to clients that opt in.

title: Handling File Uploads
objectives: Choose between uploading through the server and direct-to-storage uploads
Validate size, type and content safely
Support large files with resumable, chunked uploads

cards.title: Two paths for the bytes
cards.body: In the simple design the browser sends the file to your server in a multipart/form-data request, and the server streams it to storage. In the direct design the server issues a short-lived signed URL and the client uploads straight to object storage, so large files never pass through your application servers.

cards.title: Misconception: the file extension tells you the type
cards.body: Extensions and the client’s Content-Type header are chosen by the uploader. A file named photo.jpg can contain a script. Check size limits early, detect the type from the content, store under a generated name, and serve user files from a separate domain with a safe content type.

cards.title: A direct-to-storage upload
cards.body: Your server stays in charge of who may upload what, without carrying the bytes.
steps: Client asks the API for permission, with the file size and type
API checks limits and permissions and returns a signed URL valid for minutes
Client uploads the bytes directly to object storage
Client (or a storage event) tells the API the upload finished
API scans and processes the file in a background job

cards.title: Large files and flaky networks
cards.body: A 2 GB upload that fails at 90% should not restart from zero. Resumable or multipart uploads split the file into parts that are uploaded and retried independently, then assembled, so a failure costs one part.

cards.title: Trap: buffering uploads in memory
cards.body: Reading a whole upload into memory before saving it lets a few concurrent large uploads exhaust the server’s RAM. Enforce a maximum size at the proxy, stream bodies to storage, and prefer direct uploads for large files.

cards.title: Edge case: decompression bombs
cards.body: A small upload can expand enormously: a zip or compressed image a few megabytes in size may decompress to many gigabytes or to an image of billions of pixels. Check the declared and actual decompressed size while extracting, cap image dimensions before decoding, and process uploads in a sandbox with memory and time limits.

questions.prompt: Why issue a signed URL for direct upload to object storage?

choices.label: Signed URLs make the uploaded files smaller
It removes the need to validate the uploaded files
Large files skip your application servers while you still control access
Object storage cannot accept uploads any other way

questions.explanation: The server authorises; storage carries the bytes.

questions.prompt: How should the server decide an upload’s real file type?

choices.label: Accept any type and rename it to .txt
Trust the Content-Type header sent by the client
Trust the file extension
Inspect the content (magic bytes) and allow only expected types

questions.explanation: Uploader-supplied names and headers can lie.

questions.prompt: A 2 GB upload fails at 90% on a mobile network. Which design avoids restarting from zero?

choices.label: A single multipart/form-data request for the file
Compressing the whole file before it is uploaded
Chunked, resumable upload that retries only the failed part
Raising the server timeout to a full hour

questions.explanation: Parts are uploaded and retried independently.

questions.prompt: Where should user-uploaded files be served from?

choices.label: A separate domain, with safe content-type and download headers
The main application domain, shown inline
Any public URL that keeps the original filename
The same folder as the application code

questions.explanation: A separate origin stops an uploaded HTML or script file running with your site’s cookies.

questions.prompt: Order a direct-to-storage upload.

items.label: Client requests an upload URL
API checks size, type and permission
API returns a short-lived signed URL
API records the file and starts a scan job
Client uploads to object storage

questions.explanation: Permission first; bytes go straight to storage; processing is async.

questions.prompt: A 1.5 GB video is uploaded in 50 MB parts. The connection drops once during part 20. With resumable parts, about how many MB must be re-sent?
assumptions: 1,500 MB file, 50 MB parts
One failure inside one part
questions.explanation: Design implication: without parts, the same drop would cost re-sending everything uploaded so far (about 1 GB at part 20), so part size trades retry cost against the number of requests.

flashcards.back: Through your server (multipart) or direct to storage with a signed URL.
From the content, against an allowlist; never trust extension or Content-Type.

flashcards.front: Why a separate domain for user files?
flashcards.back: So uploaded HTML or scripts cannot run with your site’s origin and cookies.

sources.title: RFC 7578: Returning Values from Forms: multipart/form-data

mechanism.title: How an upload travels and where it is checked
steps: A browser form upload uses multipart/form-data (RFC 7578): the body contains parts separated by a boundary, each with headers such as a filename and type. Servers should stream parts to disk or storage rather than buffering them in memory.
Enforce limits as early as possible: maximum body size at the reverse proxy, which responds 413 Content Too Large, and per-user quotas in the API before issuing upload permission.

Direct uploads use a pre-signed URL: a storage URL with an expiry and a signature generated with the server’s credentials. It can restrict the method, the key (path) and sometimes the size and content type. The client never sees your storage credentials.

Validation follows OWASP’s guidance: allowlist extensions and detect the real type from the content, generate your own file names (never use the uploaded name as a path), limit size, scan for malware where relevant, and strip metadata from images if it can contain personal data such as location.
Serve user content from a separate domain or with Content-Disposition: attachment and a correct, non-executable content type, so an uploaded HTML file cannot run scripts with your site’s cookies.

Large uploads use multipart or resumable protocols: the client uploads numbered parts, each acknowledged, and completes the upload with a final call. Interrupted uploads resume from the last acknowledged part.

useWhen: Direct-to-storage uploads with signed URLs for large or frequent files.
Resumable, chunked uploads for files over tens of megabytes or on mobile networks.
avoidWhen: Avoid storing uploads on application servers’ local disks; they are not shared and not durable.
Avoid serving user files inline from your main domain.

numbers.title: Why large uploads should bypass app servers
assumptions: 200 users upload 500 MB videos in the same hour (illustrative)
Each upload takes about 10 minutes on users’ connections
steps: Data in that hour: 200 × 500 MB = 100 GB through whatever receives the uploads.
Concurrent uploads: 200 uploads × 10 minutes ÷ 60 minutes ≈ 33 at any moment on average.
Through app servers, each of those holds a connection and worker for 10 minutes, and buffering in memory would need up to 33 × 500 MB ≈ 16 GB.
With direct uploads, app servers only issue 200 signed URLs, a few milliseconds each.
numbers.result: Direct uploads turn 100 GB and dozens of long-held connections per hour into a few hundred quick API calls for your servers.

india.title: OWASP file upload guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet lists the controls in this lesson: an allowlist of extensions, validation of the file type from content, generated file names, size limits, storage outside the web root or on a separate server, authentication before upload, and serving files with safe headers. It notes that upload features are a common route to remote code execution and stored cross-site scripting when these controls are missing.

pitfalls.trap: “We check the extension, so only images get in.”
pitfalls.say: “Extensions lie; I’d check the content against an allowlist, rename the file and serve it from a separate domain.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just raise the body size limit for big videos.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d send large files straight to storage with signed URLs and use resumable parts.”

takeaways: Upload through the server for small files; direct to storage for large ones.
Check size early; detect type from content; generate names.
Serve user files from a separate domain with safe headers.
Resumable parts make large uploads survive bad networks.

interactive.title: What should the API check before signing the URL?
interactive.prompt: A client asks for a signed URL to upload a 12 GB file called report.pdf. Your limit is 2 GB and the user has 500 MB of quota left.

choices.label: Refuse: the size exceeds both the file limit and the user’s quota
choices.feedback: Right: check limits before granting permission, and bind the size into the signature where the storage supports it.

choices.label: Sign it; storage will reject oversized files anyway
choices.feedback: Only if the signature restricts size; otherwise you pay to store 12 GB.

choices.label: Sign it, because the extension is .pdf
choices.feedback: The extension says nothing about size or real content.

interactive.reveal: The API is the gatekeeper for direct uploads: check size, type and quota, then issue a short-lived URL restricted to one key (and size where supported). Validate the actual content after upload.

title: Rate Limiting in a Backend
objectives: Choose what to key a limit on and where to enforce it
Respond with 429, Retry-After and remaining-quota headers
Keep counters correct across many servers

cards.title: Who is being limited?
cards.body: A limit needs a key: an API key or account for authenticated traffic, an IP address (or network prefix) for anonymous traffic, sometimes both. Per-account limits are fair to customers; per-IP limits catch abuse before login, but many users can share one IP behind a carrier or office network.

cards.title: Misconception: a fixed window gives a smooth rate
cards.body: A limit of 100 per minute, counted in calendar minutes, lets a client send 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00: 200 in two seconds. Sliding windows or token buckets smooth this; the Rate Limiting Algorithms lesson compares them.

cards.title: Answering a limited request
cards.body: A rejected request should cost little and tell the client what to do.
steps: Look up the counter for the key (shared store, one round trip)
Under the limit: increment and continue
Over the limit: return 429 Too Many Requests immediately
Include Retry-After, and optionally the remaining quota and reset time
Log and count rejections per key for abuse monitoring

cards.title: Counters shared by every server
cards.body: With ten servers each counting on their own, a client spread across them gets ten times the limit. Keep counters in a shared fast store with atomic increments and expiry, or enforce at a single gateway layer in front of the servers.

cards.title: Trap: failing closed when the counter store is down
cards.body: If every request needs the rate-limit store and the store goes down, rejecting all traffic turns a small outage into a full one. Decide in advance: most services fail open (allow, with local fallback limits) for ordinary endpoints and fail closed only for abuse-prone ones such as login.

cards.title: Edge case: clients that retry 429s at once
cards.body: A client that retries a 429 immediately turns one rejection into a stream of them and burns its own quota faster. Send Retry-After (or rate-limit headers showing when the window resets), and make client libraries honour it with backoff. Count rejected requests separately so you can see clients in a retry loop.

questions.prompt: Which status code tells a client it has sent too many requests?

choices.label: 429 Too Many Requests
400 Bad Request
503 Service Unavailable
403 Forbidden

questions.explanation: RFC 6585 defines 429; add Retry-After so clients know when to come back.

questions.prompt: Why can a strict per-IP limit hurt legitimate users?

choices.label: IP addresses change on every single request
Many users can share one public IP behind a carrier or office network
Per-IP counters cannot be shared across servers
Servers cannot see client IP addresses at all

questions.explanation: Shared NAT addresses group many people under one IP.

questions.prompt: Limit: 100 per calendar minute. What is the worst burst a client can send within about two seconds?

choices.label: 100 requests
6,000 requests
200 requests
101 requests

questions.explanation: 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next.

questions.prompt: Ten servers each enforce “100 per minute” with local counters. A client is load-balanced evenly. What limit does it effectively get?

choices.label: Unlimited
About 1,000 per minute
100 per minute
10 per minute

questions.explanation: Each server counts only its share; shared counters fix this.

questions.prompt: Order the handling of a request under rate limiting.

items.label: Atomically increment the shared counter
Otherwise continue to the handler
Identify the key (API key or IP)
Reject with 429 and Retry-After if over
Compare with the limit

questions.explanation: Check cheaply before doing real work.

questions.prompt: Rate limiting for a public API on 12 servers.
constraints: Limits are per API key
Must stay up if the counter store has a brief outage
Login endpoint is a brute-force target

approaches.label: Shared counter store with atomic increments; fail open with local limits for normal endpoints, fail closed for login
Shared store; reject all traffic if it is down
Local counters on each server only

rationaleOptions.label: Shared atomic counters give each key its true limit across servers
Local counters are accurate if the load balancer is fair
Failing open keeps the API up during a store outage, while login stays protected

rationaleConflicts.r3: Each server still sees only a share, so the effective limit multiplies.

questions.explanation: Share counters for correctness and choose fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint.

flashcards.back: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After.
Up to twice the limit across a window boundary.
Shared atomic counters or a single enforcing gateway.

sources.title: IETF draft: RateLimit header fields for HTTP

mechanism.title: How a rate limit is enforced inside a service
steps: A rate limit protects a shared resource from one client using too much of it, and protects the service from abuse such as credential stuffing or scraping. Decide what the limit protects first, because that decides the key and the number.

Keys: authenticated traffic is limited per API key, account or tenant; anonymous traffic per IP address or network prefix; expensive endpoints may get their own lower limits. Combining keys (per account and per IP) catches both heavy customers and attackers rotating accounts.

Enforcement point: an API gateway or reverse proxy can reject excess traffic before it reaches application servers; in-app enforcement can use richer context, such as the account’s plan. Many systems do both, with a coarse limit at the edge and finer ones in the app.

Counting across servers needs a shared store that supports atomic increment with expiry. Each check costs a round trip, so keep the store close, and consider local pre-counting that syncs periodically when exactness matters less than latency.

Responses: 429 Too Many Requests (RFC 6585) with a Retry-After header. The IETF RateLimit header draft defines fields that tell clients their policy and remaining quota, so well-behaved clients can slow down before being rejected.

Failure policy: if the counter store is unreachable, fail open (allow) or fail closed (reject). Failing open with a conservative local limit is the common default; login and other abuse-sensitive endpoints may fail closed.

useWhen: Per-key limits enforced with shared atomic counters, plus a coarse edge limit for floods.
Clear 429 responses with Retry-After and quota headers for API clients.
avoidWhen: Avoid per-server local limits when exact per-client limits matter.
Avoid strict per-IP limits on endpoints used by many people behind shared addresses.

rows: Two configurations to keep in sync

numbers.title: Cost of checking the counter
assumptions: 20,000 requests per second across the API (example)
One atomic increment per request in a shared in-memory store, about 0.3 ms round trip (example)
steps: Store load: 20,000 increments per second, one per request.
Added latency: about 0.3 ms per request.
Counters needed: one per active key per window, for example 50,000 active keys means 50,000 small counters with expiry.
Local pre-counting in batches of 10 would cut store traffic to about 2,000 operations per second at the cost of slightly inexact limits.
numbers.result: Under these assumptions a shared counter adds a fraction of a millisecond and a predictable load; batching trades exactness for fewer round trips.

india.title: The RateLimit header draft
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The IETF HTTP APIs working group’s draft “RateLimit header fields for HTTP” defines response fields that describe the quota policy and how much remains in the current window. The goal is that clients can see they are approaching a limit and slow down, instead of discovering it through 429 errors. Until it is finalised, many APIs send similar custom headers, but 429 with Retry-After is already standard.

pitfalls.trap: “We limit to 100 per minute, so the rate is smooth.”
pitfalls.say: “A fixed window allows 200 across a boundary; I’d use a sliding window or token bucket if smoothness matters.”

pitfalls.trap: “Each server enforces the limit itself.”
pitfalls.say: “Then the limit multiplies by the server count; I’d use shared atomic counters or enforce at the gateway.”

takeaways: Pick the key (account, API key, IP) from what the limit protects.
Reject with 429 and Retry-After, cheaply and early.
Share counters across servers with atomic increments.
Decide fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint in advance.

interactive.title: Size the bucket
interactive.prompt: A token bucket refills at 10 tokens a second. A mobile app sends a burst of 50 requests when it opens. Slide the bucket capacity.
interactive.takeaway: Capacity decides how big a burst passes at once; the refill rate decides the long-run ceiling. With capacity 50 the app’s opening burst gets through, yet any client is still held to about 650 requests in its first minute and 10 a second after that.

title: Untrusted Input and Injection
objectives: Explain how injection turns data into commands
Use parameterised queries and avoid shells
Block path traversal and limit the damage with least privilege

cards.title: Data that becomes code
cards.body: Injection happens when untrusted input is pasted into something that will be interpreted: a database query, a shell command, a file path, a template. The interpreter cannot tell your text from the attacker’s, so the attacker’s text runs as instructions.

cards.title: Misconception: escaping quotes is enough
cards.body: Hand-written escaping misses cases: numeric contexts with no quotes, different database dialects, character set tricks. Parameterised queries send the query text and the values separately, so values are never parsed as SQL at all.

cards.title: An injected login query
cards.body: The attack works only because the query is built by joining strings.
steps: Code builds: SELECT … WHERE name = '<input>' AND pass_hash = …
Attacker enters: admin' --
Query becomes: … WHERE name = 'admin' -- ' AND pass_hash = …
The rest of the line is a comment, so the password check disappears
With a bound parameter marker, the input is just an odd user name

cards.title: Paths and shells
cards.body: A file name like ../../etc/passwd climbs out of the upload folder unless you resolve the full path and check it is still inside the allowed directory. Running a shell with user input invites command injection; call programs directly with an argument list, or better, use a library instead of a command.

cards.title: Trap: an all-powerful database user
cards.body: If the application connects as a database superuser, a single injection can drop tables or read every schema. Connect with an account that has only the permissions the application needs, so a bug cannot do more than the app could.

cards.title: Edge case: second-order injection
cards.body: Input can be stored safely with bound parameters and still cause injection later, when another component reads it back and concatenates it into a query, a shell command or HTML. Every place that builds a query or command must treat data from its own database as untrusted too.

questions.prompt: What is the main defence against SQL injection?

choices.label: Parameterised queries (prepared statements) with bound values
Hiding database error messages from the client
Escaping single quotes in the input by hand
Limiting every input to at most 50 characters

questions.explanation: Values sent separately are never parsed as SQL.

questions.prompt: A download endpoint joins the requested name to /data/uploads/. Which request is the attack?

choices.label: name=a.txt
name=../../etc/passwd
name=photo%20one.jpg
name=report-2026.pdf

questions.explanation: Dot-dot segments climb out of the intended folder.

questions.prompt: Which of these is also an injection risk?

choices.label: Returning user input as JSON with correct encoding
Hashing user input with a password hash
Storing user input in a database column with a bound parameter
Passing user input to a shell command string

questions.explanation: A shell interprets special characters as commands.

questions.prompt: Why should the app’s database account lack DROP and admin rights?

choices.label: A successful injection can then do only what the app could do
It makes the application’s queries run faster
Parameterised queries require a restricted account
Databases forbid admin accounts for applications

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits damage when another defence fails.

questions.prompt: Order a safe file download by name.

items.label: Check the resolved path is still inside the base folder
Reject names that are not on the expected pattern
Open and stream the file
Join the name to the allowed base folder
Resolve the full, normalised path

questions.explanation: Validate, resolve, confirm containment, then read.

questions.prompt: A report screen lets users sort by a column they pick.
constraints: Column names cannot be bound as query parameters
Users pick from 6 columns
Input arrives as a string

approaches.label: Insert the string into ORDER BY after escaping quotes
Map the input to an allowlist of 6 known column names
Reject inputs containing spaces

rationaleOptions.label: Escaping quotes makes identifiers safe
Anything else is rejected before the database sees it
Only known identifiers ever reach the query

rationaleConflicts.r3: Identifiers are not quoted strings, so quote escaping does not stop injection there.

questions.explanation: Bind values; allowlist identifiers such as column names and sort directions.

flashcards.back: Untrusted input is interpreted as instructions by a query, shell, path or template.
Parameterised queries; allowlist identifiers.
Resolve the full path and check it stays inside the allowed folder.

sources.title: OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
OWASP: OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: Why injection works and how each defence stops it
steps: Every interpreter has a grammar. When a program builds input for it by concatenating strings, characters with special meaning in that grammar (quotes, semicolons, comment markers, dot-dot path segments, shell metacharacters) let input change the structure of the command, not just its values.

Parameterised queries fix SQL injection at the root: the query text with parameter markers is sent and parsed first, and values are sent separately and bound to those markers. The database never interprets a value as SQL. Stored procedures are only safe if they also avoid building dynamic SQL inside.
Some parts of a query cannot be parameters: table names, column names, sort direction. Map user choices to an allowlist of known identifiers in code.

Command injection is best avoided by not using a shell: use a library function for the task, or call the program directly with an argument array so no shell parses the input. If a shell is unavoidable, allowlist the input strictly.

Path traversal is prevented by never using raw input as a path. Use generated identifiers to look files up, or resolve the full path and check it starts with the allowed base directory after normalisation, which also handles encoded and symbolic-link tricks.

Defence in depth limits the damage of the bug you missed: least-privilege database accounts, read-only file system mounts where possible, generic error messages to clients, and monitoring for unusual query errors.

useWhen: Parameterised queries everywhere values meet SQL, including in data-access libraries.
Allowlists for identifiers, file names and command arguments.
avoidWhen: Avoid building queries, commands or paths by string concatenation with input.
Avoid connecting the application as a database administrator.

rows: No shell; direct calls with argument lists
Generated ids, or resolve and check containment

numbers.title: How much a least-privilege account limits damage
assumptions: A database has 40 tables; the application needs read and write on 12 of them (illustrative)
An injection bug exists in one query
steps: As superuser: the attacker can read or drop all 40 tables and possibly reach the host.
As a least-privilege account: at most the 12 tables, and no DROP or schema changes.
With row-level permissions or separate accounts per service, the reach shrinks further.
The injection still needs fixing; privilege only bounds its blast radius.
numbers.result: Least privilege does not prevent injection, but it can cut what one bug exposes from the whole database to the slice the app already uses.

india.title: Injection in the OWASP Top 10
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Injection has been in every edition of the OWASP Top 10; in the 2021 edition it is third and includes cross-site scripting. OWASP’s SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet lists parameterised queries as the primary defence, with allowlist validation for parts that cannot be parameterised, and least privilege as an additional defence. Its command-injection guidance starts with “avoid calling OS commands directly” for the same reason.

pitfalls.trap: “We escape quotes, so we are safe from SQL injection.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d use parameterised queries for values and allowlists for identifiers; hand escaping misses cases.”

pitfalls.trap: “The input is validated in the browser.”
pitfalls.say: “Attackers send requests directly; the server binds parameters regardless of what the browser checked.”

takeaways: Injection: input changes the structure of a query, command or path.
Bind values with parameterised queries; allowlist identifiers.
Avoid shells; resolve and contain file paths.
Least privilege bounds the damage of a missed bug.

interactive.title: What does this input do?
interactive.prompt: A login query is built as: … WHERE name = '<name>' AND pass_hash = '<hash>'. An attacker types the user name admin' -- (with a trailing space).

choices.label: Logs in as admin: the rest of the query becomes a comment
choices.feedback: Right: the quote closes the string and -- comments out the password check.

choices.label: Fails, because the user name contains a quote
choices.feedback: A quote is harmless only when the query is parameterised. Here the string is built by joining text, so the quote ends the SQL string literal.

choices.label: Creates a new user called admin
choices.feedback: Nothing inserts a user here; the attack removes the password condition.

interactive.reveal: With a parameterised query the input is just a strange user name that matches nobody. Never build SQL by joining strings with input.

title: HTTP Caching and Conditional Requests
objectives: Choose Cache-Control directives for public, private and changing responses
Use ETags and conditional requests to revalidate cheaply
Avoid caching personal data in shared caches

cards.title: Freshness, then validation
cards.body: A server can let browsers and shared caches reuse a response without asking again. Cache-Control: max-age=600 says the copy is fresh for 600 seconds. Once it is stale, the cache does not have to download it again: it can ask the server whether its copy is still current.

cards.title: Misconception: no-cache means do not store
cards.body: Cache-Control: no-cache allows a cache to store the response but requires it to revalidate with the server before each reuse. The directive that forbids storing is no-store. Mixing them up either leaks sensitive data into caches or throws away cheap revalidation.

cards.title: A conditional GET with an ETag
cards.body: Revalidation sends only headers when nothing changed.
steps: First response: 200 OK, ETag: "v42", Cache-Control: max-age=600, plus the full body
For 600 seconds the client reuses its copy without any request
After that it sends GET with If-None-Match: "v42"
Unchanged: the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the copy is fresh again
Changed: the server replies 200 with the new body and a new ETag

cards.title: Lost updates and If-Match
cards.body: ETags also protect writes. A client sends PUT with If-Match: "v42"; if someone else changed the resource first, its ETag no longer matches and the server answers 412 Precondition Failed instead of silently overwriting the other change.

cards.title: Trap: a shared cache storing personal pages
cards.body: A CDN or proxy is shared by many users. If an account page goes out with Cache-Control: public or a long s-maxage, one user’s data can be served to the next. Mark per-user responses private (or no-store for sensitive data), and use Vary when the response depends on a request header.

questions.prompt: Which directive stops any cache from keeping a copy of a bank statement response?

choices.label: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: no-cache
Cache-Control: max-age=0
Cache-Control: must-revalidate

questions.explanation: no-store forbids storing; no-cache and max-age=0 still allow a stored copy that is revalidated.

questions.prompt: A client revalidates with If-None-Match and the resource has not changed. What does the server send?

choices.label: 200 OK with the full body and the same ETag
304 Not Modified with headers and no body
204 No Content with a new ETag value
412 Precondition Failed with no body

questions.explanation: 304 tells the client its stored copy is still current, so no body is sent.

questions.prompt: Two editors load a document with ETag "v7". The first saves with If-Match: "v7". What should happen when the second saves with the same header?

choices.label: The save succeeds and replaces the first editor’s text
The server merges both edits line by line
The server rejects it with 412 Precondition Failed
The server returns 304 Not Modified

questions.explanation: After the first save the ETag changed, so the precondition fails and the lost update is prevented.

questions.prompt: An API response depends on the Accept-Language header and sits behind a CDN. What must the response include so each language is cached separately?

choices.label: Vary: Accept-Language
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
An ETag built from the request URL
Content-Language: en

questions.explanation: Vary tells caches which request headers form part of the cache key.

questions.prompt: Order what a browser does when it needs a cached image again.

items.label: If stale, send a request with If-None-Match
Look up the stored copy
On 304, reuse the stored body and update its freshness
If still fresh, use it with no request

questions.explanation: Check freshness first; only stale copies trigger a conditional request.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a resource every 60 seconds for one hour, starting at second 0. The response has max-age=600 and the client caches it. How many requests reach the server in that hour?
assumptions: Requests at 0, 60, 120 … 3,540 seconds
Each server response is fresh for 600 s
questions.explanation: Design implication: freshness cut 60 requests to 6, and if those 6 are conditional most of them are bodiless 304s, so the origin pays mostly for headers.

flashcards.back: no-cache: store but revalidate before reuse. no-store: do not store.
Asks for the body only if the ETag changed; otherwise 304.
Lost updates: the write fails with 412 if the resource changed.

mechanism.title: How HTTP caches decide to reuse, revalidate or refetch
steps: A cache stores a response under a key built from the method and URL, plus any request headers named in Vary. Browsers have a private cache per user; CDNs and reverse proxies are shared caches that serve many users from one copy.

Freshness comes from Cache-Control: max-age gives seconds of freshness for any cache, s-maxage overrides it for shared caches only. While a copy is fresh, the cache answers without contacting the server. Without explicit freshness, caches may apply a heuristic based on Last-Modified, which is why important responses should state their policy.

When a copy goes stale, the cache can revalidate: it sends the request with If-None-Match (carrying the stored ETag) or If-Modified-Since (carrying Last-Modified). If nothing changed, the server sends 304 Not Modified with no body, and the cache refreshes the copy’s freshness from the new headers.

An ETag is an opaque version tag chosen by the server: a content hash or a version number from the database. Strong ETags mean byte-identical; weak ETags (W/"...") mean semantically equivalent and are used for revalidation, not for byte-range requests.

The same validators guard writes. If-Match on PUT, PATCH or DELETE makes the server apply the change only if the current ETag matches, otherwise 412 Precondition Failed. This is optimistic concurrency over HTTP.

A common pattern for static files is a content hash in the file name with a very long max-age and immutable, while the HTML that references them uses no-cache so a deploy is picked up on the next revalidation.

useWhen: Public, slowly changing responses such as product pages, images and configuration: explicit max-age plus an ETag.
Resources edited by several clients: If-Match to prevent lost updates.
avoidWhen: Avoid public or s-maxage on responses that contain one user’s data.
Avoid long max-age on URLs whose content changes in place without a new name.

rows: Each use downloads the full body
Each use, but unchanged responses are a 304 without a body
At most one revalidation per N seconds per cache
Hashed file name + long max-age, immutable
Only on first use of each version
None: a new version gets a new URL

numbers.title: What revalidation saves on bandwidth
assumptions: An API response body of 200 KB (illustrative)
A 304 response of about 300 bytes of headers (illustrative)
10,000 revalidations per minute, 95% unchanged
steps: Without validators: 10,000 × 200 KB = 2,000,000 KB, about 2 GB per minute.
With ETags: 9,500 × 0.3 KB ≈ 2,850 KB for the 304s.
The 500 changed responses still send 500 × 200 KB = 100,000 KB, about 100 MB.
Total is about 103 MB per minute instead of 2 GB.
numbers.result: Under these assumptions, conditional requests cut transfer by about 95%. The request count is unchanged, so server CPU still matters; max-age is what removes requests.

india.title: What RFC 9111 says about shared caches and Authorization
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 9111 states that a shared cache must not use a stored response to a request carrying an Authorization header unless the response explicitly allows it, for example with public, s-maxage or must-revalidate. It also defines private, which allows only the user’s own cache to store the response. RFC 9110 defines If-None-Match, If-Match and 412 Precondition Failed. Together they mean safety comes from explicit headers, not from hoping a CDN guesses correctly.

pitfalls.trap: “no-cache disables caching.”
pitfalls.say: “no-cache means revalidate before reuse; I’d use no-store when the data must not be stored.”

pitfalls.trap: “The CDN will figure out which pages are personal.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d mark per-user responses private and add Vary for headers that change the response.”

takeaways: max-age removes requests; ETags make the remaining ones cheap.
304 Not Modified has no body.
If-Match turns ETags into protection against lost updates.
Personal data: private or no-store, not public.

interactive.title: Which header leaks data?
interactive.prompt: An account page is served through a CDN. Which response header can show one user’s page to another user?

choices.label: Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300
choices.feedback: Right: the shared cache may store it for 300 seconds and serve it to anyone who requests that URL.

choices.label: Cache-Control: private, max-age=300
choices.feedback: private allows only the user’s own browser cache to store it.

choices.label: Cache-Control: no-store
choices.feedback: no-store forbids any cache from storing it.

interactive.reveal: Shared caches key responses by URL and Vary headers, not by who is logged in. Per-user responses need private or no-store; public and s-maxage are for content that is the same for everyone.
